01foundation

Scalars, Vectors & Matrices

One number, a list, a grid. That is the whole cast.

A scalar is one number. A vector is a list of numbers kept in order, and the order is the whole point — slot three always means the same thing. A matrix is a grid: rows and columns of numbers. Nothing here is mysterious. The only thing that changes as you climb is how many labels you need to point at one number: none, then one, then two.

Like a recipe card. One number is the 200 grams of flour. A vector is the whole ingredient list in a fixed order, so slot one is always flour. A matrix is a dozen recipes stacked into a table — one row per recipe, one column per ingredient.

A scalar is a rank-0 tensor, a vector v∈Rn is rank-1, a matrix A∈Rm×n is rank-2: each step adds one index, and in code each step adds one entry to .shape. Two conventions to lock in now. Vectors are columns by default, so Av reads (m×n)(n×1)→(m×1). And everything in a deep-learning stack carries a leading batch dimension, so the “vector” of activations you are picturing is really shape (B, d). Most shape bugs are one of those two being violated quietly.

Shapes are the type system of ML. (3,), (3,1) and (1,3) hold the same three numbers and behave completely differently: (3,1) + (1,3) broadcasts to a 3×3 matrix instead of raising. NumPy’s 1-D array is neither a row nor a column — it is a third thing that changes meaning depending on which side of @ it sits.

You reach for it when

  • Reading a paper and needing to know the shape of every symbol
  • A layer throws a shape error and you have to say what it wanted
  • Deciding between a list of lists and one real array
  • Someone says “tensor” and you need to know if they mean anything deeper

The trap

rank means two unrelated things. To NumPy and PyTorch it is the number of indices — ndim. In linear algebra it is the number of independent directions the matrix actually spans. A (1000, 1000) array is rank-2 to the library and can still be rank 1 in the sense that matters. Always ask which one they mean.

The math shapes, not cost

s∈R  ·  v∈Rn  ·  A∈Rm×n  ·  T∈Rb×m×nA column vector is n×1; a row vector is v⊤, shape 1×n. Av is legal only when the inner dimensions touch: (m×n)(n×1).

In NumPy / PyTorch

import numpy as np

s = np.float32(3.0)          # scalar  shape ()
v = np.array([1., 2., 3.])    # vector  shape (3,)
A = np.zeros((4, 3))      # matrix  shape (4, 3)
T = np.zeros((8, 4, 3))   # batch of matrices  (8, 4, 3)

A @ v                     # (4,3) @ (3,) -> (4,)  fine
v[:, None].shape          # (3, 1)  an explicit column
v[None, :] + v[:, None]   # (1,3)+(3,1) -> (3,3)  silent bug

Where this lives in real ML code

Every Hugging Face model signature is a shape contract: input_ids is (batch, seq), hidden states are (batch, seq, d_model), logits are (batch, seq, vocab). Feed one un-batched sentence of shape (seq,) and the forward pass either crashes on the spot or treats your tokens as a batch of single-token rows and hands back confident nonsense.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

A colleague says their tensor is “rank 3”. What did they mean, and what else could it have meant?
They meant three indices — ndim == 3, something like (batch, seq, d). Linear-algebra rank is the number of linearly independent rows or columns, a property of the values, not the shape. A 1000×1000 matrix of all ones has ndim 2 and rank 1.
What is the difference between shape (3,), (3,1) and (1,3)?
One is a 1-D array, the other two are 2-D. (3,1) is a column, (1,3) is a row, and (3,) is neither — it takes whichever role the operator needs. The bite is broadcasting: adding a (3,1) to a (1,3) gives a (3,3) outer sum with no error at all.
Say out loud what a matrix is, without using the word grid.
A matrix is a machine that takes a vector in and gives a vector out, and it does it linearly — scaling the input scales the output, adding inputs adds outputs. The grid of numbers is just where the machine keeps its settings: column j tells you where the j-th input axis lands. That sentence is what the rest of this page unpacks.

Say this back tomorrow

scalar → vector → matrix → tensor = 0, 1, 2, n indices
  • A vector is a column unless someone tells you otherwise.
  • Shape is the type. Say it out loud on every line and half your bugs vanish.
  • ndim is not linear-algebra rank. Different words, same spelling.

Unlocks

  • shape
  • ndim vs rank
  • broadcasting
  • column vector
  • batch dimension

02foundation

Vector Addition & Scaling

Two moves. Everything else is built from them.

Adding two lists means adding them slot by slot: first with first, second with second. Picture it as arrows — take one walk, then start the second walk from wherever the first one left you, and the sum is the straight arrow from start to finish. Scaling means multiplying every slot by the same number, which keeps the direction and only changes the length. A negative number turns the arrow around. Every linear layer in every model you have ever run is those two moves, a few million times.

Like following two sets of walking directions back to back. Four blocks east, then two blocks north, puts you exactly where one diagonal shortcut would have: same finish, and the shortcut is the sum. Scaling is walking down that same street for twice as long.

Addition is elementwise, (u+v)i​=ui​+vi​, and scaling is (αv)i​=αvi​. Those two closed operations are the definition of a vector space, and a function that respects both is linear: f(αu+βv)=αf(u)+βf(v). That single property is why a whole layer can be stored as a matrix instead of as code. Geometrically, addition is tip-to-tail translation and scaling slides a vector along the line through the origin, flipping it when α<0. A linear combination ∑i​αi​vi​ is both moves at once, and it is the only thing a linear layer ever computes.

Watch the origin. Neither move can shift it, so f(0)=0 for any linear map — which means a layer with a bias is affine, not linear. That is not pedantry: it is why we sometimes append a constant-one column to the input and fold b into W, and it is why a linearity unit test on nn.Linear(4, 4) fails until you pass bias=False.

You reach for it when

  • Combining two embeddings into one vector
  • Reading what a residual connection actually adds
  • Turning a learning rate into a step you can picture
  • Checking whether an operation is really linear

The trap

Adding two unit vectors does not give you a unit vector, and averaging embeddings shrinks them towards the middle — the mean of many unit vectors is shorter than one, and gets shorter the less they agree. If a downstream step assumes unit length, re-normalise after you add. Second trap: a layer with a bias is affine, so it will fail any linearity check you write.

The math O(n) work, O(n) memory, no data movement worth worrying about

u+v=[u1​+v1​, …, un​+vn​]  ·  αv=[αv1​, …, αvn​]Linear combination: ∑i​αi​vi​. Linearity test: f(αu+βv)=αf(u)+βf(v), which forces f(0)=0 — so Wx+b is affine, not linear.

In NumPy / PyTorch

u = np.array([3., 1.]); v = np.array([1., 2.])

u + v                # [4., 3.]   tip to tail
2.5 * u              # [7.5, 2.5] same direction, longer
u - v                # [2., -1.]  flip v, then add

w -= lr * grad       # one SGD step IS scale-and-add
h = h + attn_out     # a residual connection IS vector addition
np.mean(E, axis=0)     # mean pooling: add them all, scale by 1/n

Where this lives in real ML code

A residual connection is literally vector addition — x + sublayer(x) — and it is the reason a 100-layer transformer trains at all, because the gradient gets an unscaled path straight back down the stack. One SGD step, w -= lr * grad, is one scaling and one addition; get the sign or the scale wrong there and the loss climbs instead of falling, which is exactly what a missing optimizer.zero_grad() looks like.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Is x → Wx + b linear? Prove it in one line.
No, it is affine. Linearity needs f(0)=0 and here f(0)=b. Equivalently f(u+v)=W(u+v)+b=f(u)+f(v)−b, which only matches when b=0. We still call it a linear layer in practice; the honest fix is to append a constant-one feature and fold b into W.
You average 1000 unit-length embeddings. Roughly how long is the result?
Much shorter than one, and how much shorter tells you how aligned they were. For near-random directions in high dimensions the mean length falls off like 1/n​; for perfectly aligned vectors it stays at 1. This is why mean-pooled sentence embeddings are re-normalised before a cosine search — and why the pooled vector for a long, rambling document is short.
Explain to a non-technical colleague why scaling can never change direction.
Because every component is multiplied by the same number. If you double both the east part and the north part of a walk, the walk is twice as long but the bearing is identical — the ratio between the parts is what direction is, and a shared factor cancels out of a ratio. Multiply by a negative number and every part reverses at once, which is a U-turn, not a new bearing.

Say this back tomorrow

add = tip to tail  ·  scale = same line, new length
  • Scaling keeps direction; only a negative factor flips it, and that is still the same line.
  • A linear combination is the only thing a linear layer computes.
  • Linear means the origin cannot move. Add a bias and you are affine.

Unlocks

  • linear combination
  • span
  • residual connection
  • affine vs linear
  • mean pooling

03foundation

Dot Product

Two lists in, one agreement score out.

Line the two lists up, multiply them position by position, then add everything into a single number. That number is an agreement score. Big and positive means the two lists point the same way. Around zero means they have nothing to do with each other. Negative means they pull in opposite directions. It is the most repeated operation in machine learning by a mile, and almost everything further up this page is a pile of these.

Like two friends scoring the same ten films out of five. Multiply their scores film by film and add it all up: a big total means they agree, a small one means their tastes barely overlap.

The dot product u⋅v=∑i​ui​vi​=∥u∥∥v∥cosθ measures how much of one vector lies along the other — a projection, scaled by both lengths. Positive means an acute angle, zero means orthogonal, negative means obtuse. It is the atom of the whole stack: one entry of a matrix product, one logit in a linear layer, one score in QK⊤ before the softmax, one similarity in a vector database. The hardware agrees — a tensor core is a machine for doing thousands of these at once.

Two things to keep straight. Orthogonal (u⋅v=0) is not the same as statistically uncorrelated unless both vectors are mean-centred first, and it is stronger than merely independent. And the dot product grows with dimension: for random vectors with unit-variance entries, u⋅v has standard deviation d​, which is exactly why attention divides by dk​​ before the softmax — without it the logits are huge, the softmax saturates, and the gradient dies.

You reach for it when

  • Scoring a query against a document embedding
  • Reading one single entry of a matrix multiply
  • Checking whether two directions are orthogonal
  • Any time a model turns a whole vector into one score

The trap

The dot product is not a similarity unless you control the lengths. A long vector beats a short one even when it points somewhere less relevant, which is why raw inner-product search quietly favours long documents and popular items. Normalise first, or use cosine — and know which one your index is actually configured for.

The math O(n) multiply-adds in, exactly one number out

u⋅v=∑i=1n​ui​vi​=∥u∥∥v∥cosθu⋅v=0⟺ perpendicular. u⋅u=∥u∥2. Attention uses softmax(QK⊤/dk​​) because the dot of two random dk​-vectors grows like dk​​.

In NumPy / PyTorch

u = np.array([2., 1., 3.]); v = np.array([4., 0., 1.])

u @ v                 # 11.0  the whole card in one line
np.dot(u, v)          # 11.0  same thing
u @ u                 # 14.0  = squared L2 length of u

A @ v                 # every row of A, dotted with v
scores = Q @ K.T / d_k**0.5   # every query dotted with every key

Where this lives in real ML code

In attention, QK⊤ is nothing but every query row dotted with every key row: for a 4k-token context that is 16 million dot products per head per layer, which is the whole reason long context is expensive. On the retrieval side, faiss.IndexFlatIP scores a query against every stored vector with the identical operation — a brute-force index literally is a big pile of dot products.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Two non-zero vectors have dot product zero. Are they independent? Are they uncorrelated?
Independent yes, uncorrelated only if they are mean-centred. Orthogonality implies linear independence for non-zero vectors, but not the reverse — independent vectors can sit at any angle except 0 and 180 degrees. Correlation is the dot product of centred vectors divided by their lengths, so u⋅v=0 on raw data says nothing about correlation.
Why does attention divide the scores by dk​​?
To keep the logits at a scale the softmax can survive. With unit-variance entries, q⋅k over dk​ dimensions has variance dk​, so at dk​=128 the raw scores swing by roughly ±11. Softmax on numbers that big is effectively a hard argmax: one weight near 1, the rest near 0, and gradients near 0. Dividing by dk​​ pulls the variance back to 1.
A document scores highest by dot product but is obviously off-topic. What happened, and what do you change?
It is long, not relevant. The dot product multiplies by both magnitudes, so a vector with a big norm scores well against everything — the classic symptom is your longest chunks winning every query. Fix it by L2-normalising the embeddings (then the dot product is cosine) or by switching the index metric to cosine. Change one, not both, and measure recall afterwards.

Say this back tomorrow

u⋅v=∑i​ui​vi​=∥u∥∥v∥cosθ
  • Multiply position by position, add once, get an agreement score.
  • Zero means perpendicular. Negative means they disagree.
  • It is magnitude-sensitive: long vectors score high on everything.

Unlocks

  • inner product
  • orthogonality
  • projection
  • attention scores
  • matrix multiply

04foundation

Vector Norms (L1, L2)

How big is this thing, and whose ruler?

A norm is a ruler for a list of numbers: one number saying how big the whole list is. Two of them come up constantly. Add up the sizes of every entry, ignoring minus signs, and that is the first ruler. Square everything, add, take the square root, and that is the second — the straight-line length you would get with a piece of string. Same list, two honest answers, and they behave very differently when you use them to punish a model for growing too big.

Like a taxi versus a crow. To get three blocks east and four blocks north the taxi drives seven blocks because it has to follow the streets; the crow flies five. Both are correct answers to “how far” — they are just different rulers.

∥v∥1​=∑i​∣vi​∣ and ∥v∥2​=∑i​vi2​​ are the two to know cold. L2 is Euclidean length: smooth everywhere, and its gradient v/∥v∥2​ points straight out from the origin, so Ridge (λ∥w∥22​) shrinks every weight in proportion and drives none of them to exactly zero. L1 is not differentiable at zero and its gradient is sign(w) — a constant pull towards zero no matter how small the weight already is — so Lasso (λ∥w∥1​) produces exact zeros and hands you feature selection for free.

The geometric version is the one interviewers want. The constraint set ∥w∥1​≤t is a diamond whose corners sit on the axes, so a loss contour sliding in from outside almost always touches at a corner — and a corner means a coordinate is exactly 0. The L2 ball is a smooth sphere with no corners, so the contact point virtually never has a zero coordinate. The same norm shows up in gradient clipping: clip_grad_norm_ rescales the whole gradient, g←g⋅min(1, c/∥g∥2​), capping the length while keeping the direction intact.

You reach for it when

  • Choosing between Lasso and Ridge and having to justify it
  • Stopping exploding gradients without changing their direction
  • Turning embeddings into unit vectors before a cosine search
  • Reading a loss curve that has a penalty term bolted on

The trap

Everyone says “L1 gives sparsity” and the follow-up question is always why. The answer is geometric, not mystical: the L1 ball is a diamond, its corners lie on the axes, and a loss contour touching a corner means that coordinate is exactly zero. Ridge shrinks weights towards zero smoothly and essentially never lands on it, so it gives you small weights, never a shorter feature list.

The math O(n) either way; L2 costs one square root

∥v∥1​=∑i​∣vi​∣  ·  ∥v∥2​=∑i​vi2​​  ·  ∥v∥∞​=maxi​∣vi​∣Ridge adds λ∥w∥22​, Lasso adds λ∥w∥1​. Clipping: g←g⋅min(1, c/∥g∥2​). Always ∥v∥2​≤∥v∥1​≤n​∥v∥2​.

In NumPy / PyTorch

v = np.array([3., -4.])

np.linalg.norm(v, 1)      # 7.0  L1: 3 + 4
np.linalg.norm(v)         # 5.0  L2: sqrt(9 + 16)
v / np.linalg.norm(v)     # unit vector, length 1

# keep the direction, cap the length
torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)

Ridge(alpha=1.0)           # L2 penalty -> small weights, none exactly 0
Lasso(alpha=1.0)           # L1 penalty -> some weights exactly 0

Where this lives in real ML code

Every serious training loop has clip_grad_norm_(params, 1.0) in it: one bad batch produces a giant gradient, the L2 norm gets rescaled back to 1.0, and the direction survives so the step still points the right way. Without it the loss goes to NaN and the run is dead. On the retrieval side, faiss.normalize_L2(X) is the same norm in one line — divide by the length so an inner-product index behaves as cosine.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Why does L1 give exactly-zero weights when L2 does not?
Corners. The set ∥w∥1​≤t is a diamond and its corners sit on the axes, so the point where the loss contour first touches it is usually a corner — and a corner has a coordinate of exactly 0. In gradient terms, the L1 penalty pulls with constant force λsign(w) even as w→0, while the L2 pull 2λw fades away, so it only ever gets you small, never zero.
Your loss goes to NaN at step 400. Which norm do you reach for, and what does it actually do?
Global grad-norm clipping with L2. It computes one norm over all parameters stitched together and rescales them by min(1, c/∥g∥2​), so the direction is untouched and only the step length is capped. That is different from clip_grad_value_, which clamps each component separately and does bend the update direction. Clipping hides the symptom, so check your learning rate and any divide-by-almost-zero too.
You have 10,000 features and need to know which 50 matter. Ridge or Lasso, and what is the catch?
Lasso, because it zeroes coefficients outright and leaves you a short list. The honest caveat: with correlated features Lasso picks one of the group more or less arbitrarily and zeros its twins, so the selection is unstable across resamples. Elastic net (both penalties) keeps correlated groups together, and either way a zero coefficient means “not needed given the others”, not “unimportant”.

Say this back tomorrow

L1 =∑i​∣vi​∣ has corners  ·  L2 =∑i​vi2​​ is smooth
  • L1 sums the sizes, L2 measures the straight line.
  • Corners on the axes give exact zeros: Lasso selects, Ridge only shrinks.
  • Clipping rescales by the L2 norm: same direction, shorter step.

Unlocks

  • Lasso
  • Ridge
  • gradient clipping
  • unit vector
  • elastic net

05foundation

Cosine Similarity & Distance

Same topic, different length. Same score?

Cosine similarity throws the length away and keeps only the direction. It asks one question: are these two lists pointing the same way? You get a number between one and minus one. One means the same direction, zero means unrelated, minus one means opposite. Because length is thrown away, a long report and a short note about the same thing score the same. Cosine distance is just one minus that score, so smaller means more alike.

Like comparing two people’s music taste. One listens eight hours a day and one listens twenty minutes, but if they play the same artists in the same proportions their taste is identical. Cosine reads the proportions and ignores the hours.

cosθ=∥u∥∥v∥u⋅v​ — the dot product with both magnitudes divided out, so it lives in [−1,1] and is invariant to rescaling either vector. Cosine distance is 1−cosθ (not a true metric — it breaks the triangle inequality). The identity that matters in production: if both vectors are already L2-normalised then ∥u∥=∥v∥=1, so the cosine is the plain dot product, and ∥u−v∥22​=2−2u⋅v — Euclidean distance and cosine then rank every result identically.

That identity is why nearly every vector database normalises on ingest: store unit vectors, then use the cheapest kernel you have — inner product — and cosine ranking comes free with no per-query division. It is also the catch. Cosine is blind to magnitude on purpose, so when magnitude carries real signal (popularity, confidence, term counts, recency weighting) cosine discards it and raw inner product (MIPS) is the correct choice. Match the metric to the objective the embeddings were trained with.

You reach for it when

  • Ranking documents against a query in a vector database
  • Deduplicating near-identical embeddings
  • Comparing two texts of wildly different length
  • Choosing an index metric and having to defend the choice

The trap

Cosine ignoring magnitude is a feature right up until it is a bug: a two-line note and a fifty-page report on the same topic score identically, so cosine cannot rank by how much evidence a document holds. And never mix metrics — querying an inner-product index with un-normalised embeddings is the classic silent failure, where your longest chunks win every single query and recall quietly rots.

The math O(n) for the dot, plus two norms unless you normalised at ingest

cosθ=∥u∥2​∥v∥2​u⋅v​∈[−1,1]  ·  dcos​=1−cosθIf ∥u∥2​=∥v∥2​=1 then cosθ=u⋅v and ∥u−v∥22​=2−2cosθ — identical ranking, so normalise once at ingest and use the cheap inner product forever after.

In NumPy / PyTorch

q = np.array([3., 2.])
long_doc  = np.array([6., 2.])   # same direction, 4x longer
short_doc = np.array([1.5, 0.5])

q @ long_doc                # 22.0  the long one "wins"
q @ short_doc               # 5.5   ...only because it is longer

def cos(a, b): return a @ b / (np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b))
cos(q, long_doc)            # 0.9648
cos(q, short_doc)           # 0.9648  identical: same direction

# what a vector DB does on ingest
X /= np.linalg.norm(X, axis=1, keepdims=True)   # now inner product == cosine
index = faiss.IndexFlatIP(d)                # cheapest kernel, cosine ranking

Where this lives in real ML code

OpenAI’s embedding endpoints return vectors already normalised to length 1, which is why faiss.IndexFlatIP over them is cosine search — the standard RAG setup. The failure is real and common: index un-normalised embeddings with an inner-product metric and every query starts returning your longest chunks. pgvector makes you choose out loud with three operators — <=> cosine, <#> inner product, <-> L2 — and the operator must match the one your index was built for or it silently falls back to a sequential scan.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Your RAG system keeps returning the longest chunks for every query. What is wrong?
Un-normalised vectors in an inner-product index. The dot product scales with magnitude, so long chunks with big norms beat shorter, more relevant ones. Fix it by L2-normalising at ingest (and normalising the query too), or by switching the index metric to cosine. Also check your chunking: if one chunk is ten times the size of the rest, that is the real bug.
On unit vectors, does switching from cosine to Euclidean change your top-k?
No — the ranking is identical. For unit vectors ∥u−v∥22​=2−2u⋅v, so Euclidean distance is a strictly decreasing function of cosine similarity: sorting by one sorts by the other. The scores differ and any absolute threshold you tuned must be re-derived, but the returned set does not. Off unit vectors, all bets are off.
Explain out loud why a tweet and a whitepaper on the same topic get the same cosine score, and when that is wrong.
Because cosine divides both vectors by their own length, so only the direction — the mix of topics — survives. That is exactly what you want when you are matching subject matter across documents of different sizes. It is wrong when magnitude carries signal you care about: term counts, confidence, popularity, or recency weighting baked into the vector. Then keep the magnitude and use inner product (MIPS) instead.

Say this back tomorrow

cosθ=∥u∥∥v∥u⋅v​, and on unit vectors it is just u⋅v
  • Normalise once at ingest, then the cheap inner product gives you cosine ranking.
  • Cosine ignores magnitude on purpose. If magnitude is signal, use inner product.
  • On unit vectors, cosine and Euclidean return the same top-k in a different order of score.

Unlocks

  • unit vector
  • inner product (MIPS)
  • FAISS / pgvector
  • RAG retrieval
  • ANN index

06foundation

Matrix Multiplication & Transpose

Every layer in every network is one of these.

Take a row from the left grid and a column from the right grid, multiply them slot by slot, add up the results, and drop that one number into the answer grid. Repeat for every row and column pair until the answer is full. The only rule is that the row and the column must be the same length, or there is nothing to pair up. And order matters: swapping the two grids gives you a different answer, or no answer at all.

Like a part travelling down an assembly line. Each station reshapes what it is handed, so the tray leaving one station has to fit the tray the next one expects — and drilling before painting builds a different part than painting before drilling.

Entry (i,j) of AB is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B: (AB)ij​=∑k​Aik​Bkj​. Shapes chain and the inner dimensions cancel: (m,n)⋅(n,p)→(m,p). It is associative and distributive but not commutative — AB=BA, and usually BA is not even a legal shape. Transpose swaps indices, (A⊤)ij​=Aji​, and reverses order through a product: (AB)⊤=B⊤A⊤. A dense layer is literally this: XW+b, with X of shape (B,din​) and W of shape (din​,dout​).

Cost is O(mnp), or 2mnp flops — the number every GPU spec sheet is really quoting. Non-commutativity is not a technicality: in attention QK⊤ is (L,d)⋅(d,L)→(L,L), a token-by-token score matrix, while Q⊤K is (d,L)⋅(L,d)→(d,d), a feature-by-feature matrix. Same two tensors, completely different object, and only one of them is attention.

You reach for it when

  • Any time data meets weights — every forward pass is a stack of these.
  • Chaining transforms: rotate, then scale, then project, collapsed into one matrix.
  • Batching, so one call handles every row in the batch at once.
  • Debugging a shape error at 2am.

The trap

The error everyone hits: (64,128) @ (64,128) fails because the inner dimensions disagree — you wanted A @ B.T. The subtler one is when it succeeds and is still wrong: with a square weight matrix W @ x and x @ W both run, silently computing different things. Never assume A @ B == B @ A.

The math (m,n) @ (n,p) → (m,p) · 2mnp flops

(AB)ij​=k=1∑n​Aik​Bkj​(AB)⊤=B⊤A⊤AB=BAinner dims must match, then they vanish · outer dims become your output shape

In NumPy / PyTorch

X = np.random.randn(32, 768)      # 32 rows, 768 features
W = np.random.randn(768, 3072)    # one dense layer
H = X @ W + b                     # (32,768) @ (768,3072) -> (32,3072)

X @ X       # ValueError: 768 and 32 do not line up
X @ X.T     # (32,768) @ (768,32) -> (32,32), a gram matrix
X.T @ X     # (768,32) @ (32,768) -> (768,768), a totally different object

assert H.shape == (32, 3072)   # cheapest test you will ever write

Where this lives in real ML code

One forward pass of a 7B transformer is a few hundred of these back to back, and the @ inside q @ k.transpose(-2,-1) in every attention block is one of them. When a fine-tune dies with mat1 and mat2 shapes cannot be multiplied (32x768 and 3072x768), someone stored a weight the other way round: nn.Linear keeps W as (dout​,din​) and applies xW⊤, which is where a good half of these mismatches come from.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

You have shapes (8,64) and (64,8). Which products are legal, and what comes out?
Both are legal, and they are different objects. (8,64)⋅(64,8)→(8,8); (64,8)⋅(8,64)→(64,64), which has rank at most 8. Same two tensors, one gives you a tiny full-rank matrix and the other a big rank-deficient one. This is exactly the QK⊤ versus Q⊤K distinction, and only the first one is attention.
Explain out loud why (AB)⊤=B⊤A⊤ and not A⊤B⊤.
The shapes force it. If A is (m,n) and B is (n,p) then (AB)⊤ is (p,m). Now B⊤ is (p,n) and A⊤ is (n,m), so B⊤A⊤ chains to (p,m) — correct. A⊤B⊤ would be (n,m)⋅(p,n), illegal unless the sizes coincide by accident. Undoing an assembly line means visiting the stations in reverse order.
Your model is slow and someone suggests folding two linear layers into one matrix. When is that free, and when is it wrong?
Free only if nothing sits between them. Associativity gives (XW1​)W2​=X(W1​W2​), so two adjacent linear layers fold into one at inference time — that is exactly what LoRA merging and conv-BN fusion do. Put a ReLU in the middle and the fold is illegal: σ(XW1​)W2​=X(W1​W2​). Also check the arithmetic: folding two (d,d) matrices costs O(d3) once but saves work on every batch afterwards.

Say this back tomorrow

(m,n) @ (n,p) → (m,p) · (AB)⊤=B⊤A⊤
  • One cell of the answer = one row of the left, one column of the right, dotted.
  • The two inner numbers must match and then disappear; the outer two are your output shape.
  • AB and BA ask different questions. Transposing a product reverses the order.

Unlocks

  • dot product
  • batched matmul
  • nn.Linear
  • attention scores
  • einsum
  • transpose

07foundation

Identity, Diagonal & Orthogonal Matrices

Three matrices you can read at a glance.

Three shapes worth knowing on sight. The first does nothing at all: whatever goes in comes out untouched. The second has numbers only down the diagonal, and it stretches or shrinks each direction on its own without ever mixing them, which makes it absurdly cheap to use. The third turns or mirrors everything as one rigid piece, like spinning a photo: nothing is stretched, every distance and angle stays exactly as it was, and undoing it is free.

Like a mixing desk. The identity is every fader parked at unity, signal straight through. A diagonal matrix is one fader per channel, each moved on its own with no bleed. An orthogonal matrix swings the whole stereo image around — the instruments move, the total loudness does not.

I is the multiplicative identity: IA=AI=A. A diagonal D=diag(d1​,…,dn​) acts elementwise, so applying it is O(n) rather than O(n2), storing it is n numbers rather than n2, inverting it is n reciprocals rather than O(n3), and detD=∏i​di​. An orthogonal Q has orthonormal columns, so Q⊤Q=QQ⊤=I and therefore Q−1=Q⊤ — the inverse is free. It preserves geometry exactly: ∥Qx∥2​=∥x∥2​, ⟨Qx,Qy⟩=⟨x,y⟩, detQ=±1, and κ2​(Q)=1.

That condition number is the whole point. Every singular value of Q is exactly 1, so multiplying by Q can neither amplify rounding error nor shrink a gradient. That is why QR and Householder reflections are the numerically stable route to least squares, why orthogonal weight initialisation keeps signal norm alive through a deep or recurrent stack, and why rotations are the safe way to move data around. detQ=+1 is a rotation; detQ=−1 folds in a reflection.

You reach for it when

  • You need an inverse and you are lucky enough to have a diagonal or an orthogonal matrix.
  • Per-feature scaling: standardisation, LayerNorm gains and Adam step sizes are all diagonal.
  • Rotating a basis without distorting the data — QR, PCA loadings, rotary embeddings.
  • Initialising or constraining weights in a deep or recurrent network.

The trap

Orthogonal is a property of the whole matrix, and it needs columns that are orthonormal — unit length, not merely perpendicular. Scale one column by two and the property is gone. Worse, a tall matrix with orthonormal columns satisfies Q⊤Q=I but not QQ⊤=I: on that side it is a projection, not an undo.

The math diagonal apply O(n) · orthogonal inverse free

Ix=xDx=(d1​x1​,…,dn​xn​)Q⊤Q=QQ⊤=I⇒Q−1=Q⊤∥Qx∥2​=∥x∥2​ · detQ=±1 · κ2​(Q)=1 exactly

In NumPy / PyTorch

d = np.array([2., 0.5, 3.]);  D = np.diag(d)
D @ x                 # O(n^2) work and n^2 memory, for no reason
d * x                 # identical answer, O(n). always this.

Q, R = np.linalg.qr(np.random.randn(4, 4))
np.allclose(Q.T @ Q, np.eye(4))            # True: the inverse is just Q.T
np.allclose(norm(Q @ x), norm(x))          # True: lengths survive untouched
np.linalg.cond(Q)                          # 1.0, the best a matrix can be

torch.nn.init.orthogonal_(layer.weight)    # keeps signal norm through depth

Where this lives in real ML code

LayerNorm’s learned gain and Adam’s second-moment term are diagonal matrices that nobody ever materialises — they live as 1-D arrays and get applied with a broadcast multiply, which is the whole reason adaptive optimisers are affordable at billions of parameters. On the orthogonal side, rotary position embeddings apply a 2-D rotation to each pair of query and key dimensions exactly because a rotation moves the vector without changing its norm, so attention logits keep the same scale at position 4000 as at position 4.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Why is a diagonal matrix cheap and a general one expensive?
Because it touches each coordinate once and never mixes them. Dx is n multiplies; storage is n numbers, not n2; the inverse is n reciprocals; the determinant is ∏di​; the eigenvalues are the entries themselves. A general matrix costs O(n2) to apply and O(n3) to factor or invert. Every time a method says “assume a diagonal covariance”, this is what it is buying.
An interviewer says: prove an orthogonal matrix preserves length.
One line, and say it out loud. ∥Qx∥22​=(Qx)⊤(Qx)=x⊤Q⊤Qx=x⊤Ix=∥x∥22​. Angles come free from the same fact: ⟨Qx,Qy⟩=x⊤Q⊤Qy=⟨x,y⟩. Everything about orthogonal matrices is downstream of Q⊤Q=I.
A 512-by-64 matrix has orthonormal columns. Is it invertible? Is QQ⊤=I?
No and no. It is not square, so there is no inverse — only a left inverse, Q⊤Q=I64​. And QQ⊤ is 512×512 with rank 64: the orthogonal projection onto the 64-dimensional column space, not the identity. Push a 512-vector through Q⊤ and then Q and everything outside that subspace is gone for good. This is exactly what an autoencoder bottleneck does.

Say this back tomorrow

Q−1=Q⊤ · ∥Qx∥=∥x∥ · κ(Q)=1
  • Identity: the do-nothing matrix, and the thing every “undo” has to produce.
  • Diagonal: one independent knob per axis. O(n) to apply, invert and take the determinant.
  • Orthogonal: a rigid turn or mirror. Free inverse, zero distortion, no error amplification.

Unlocks

  • QR decomposition
  • Householder reflection
  • rotation matrix
  • orthogonal init
  • condition number
  • rotary embeddings

08foundation

Systems of Linear Equations

Many rules at once, and the point that obeys them all.

Each equation is a rule, and one rule on its own rules out almost everything, leaving a whole line of survivors. Put two rules together and usually a single point survives both: that is your answer. Two things can go wrong. The rules can contradict each other, so nothing survives and there is no answer at all. Or the second rule can just repeat the first, so it removes nothing and an endless line of answers survives.

Like two currency receipts. One receipt saying a pile of dollars and yen came to five hundred euros leaves endless possibilities. A second receipt at different rates pins down exactly how much of each you handed over — unless that booth used the very same rates, in which case the second receipt tells you nothing you did not already know.

Stack the constraints and the whole thing is one object: Ax=b. Row picture — every row is a hyperplane and the solution set is their intersection. Column picture, the one that matters in ML — which combination of A’s columns lands exactly on b? Rank settles the outcome: unique when rank(A)=rank([A∣b])=n, infinitely many when that shared rank is <n (free variables are left over), and none at all when rank(A)<rank([A∣b]), meaning b sits outside the column space.

In practice m=n. Overdetermined (m>n: more data than parameters) is the normal ML case and is almost always inconsistent, so you stop demanding equality and minimise ∥Ax−b∥2​ instead — that is linear regression, and the answer is the projection of b onto the column space. Underdetermined (m<n: more parameters than data) has an infinite family, so you pick one with a preference: minimum norm, ridge, or lasso.

You reach for it when

  • Fitting anything in closed form: normal equations, ridge, Kalman updates, GP posteriors.
  • Any question shaped like “find the weights that make these outputs come out right”.
  • Backing out a transform when you can only see what it did.
  • Checking whether a set of constraints is satisfiable at all before you optimise over it.

The trap

A square system is not automatically solvable, and “no exact solution” is not an error — it is the normal condition of real data. The interview trap: with m>n there is usually no solution to Ax=b at all, yet lstsq happily returns one. Know which question you asked. And near-singular is nastier than singular: it returns a confident answer that is mostly amplified noise.

The math m equations, n unknowns · rank decides

Ax=b⟹⎩⎨⎧​oneinfinitenone​rank(A)=rank([A∣b])=nrank(A)=rank([A∣b])<nrank(A)<rank([A∣b])​no exact solution? stop demanding equality and minimise the residual instead

In NumPy / PyTorch

A = np.array([[2., 1.], [1., 3.]]);  b = np.array([5., 10.])
x = np.linalg.solve(A, b)          # square and non-singular -> one exact answer

X = np.random.randn(1000, 5)       # 1000 constraints, 5 unknowns
y = np.random.randn(1000)
np.linalg.solve(X, y)              # LinAlgError: last 2 dims must be square
w, res, rank, sv = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)   # this is linear regression
rank                               # < 5 means your features are collinear

Where this lives in real ML code

Closed-form linear regression is exactly this: sklearn’s LinearRegression hands X and y to LAPACK’s gelsd least-squares driver rather than solving anything exactly, because with a thousand rows and five columns no exact solution exists. Where it bites in production is collinear features: two near-duplicate columns make the system nearly rank-deficient, the coefficients swing wildly between retrains on almost identical data, and every accuracy metric on your dashboard looks completely fine.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Three equations, two unknowns. What do you expect?
Usually no exact solution. Three lines in a plane rarely pass through one point. It is consistent only if the third constraint happens to hit the intersection of the first two — formally, only if b lies in the column space of A. Otherwise you change the question and minimise ∥Ax−b∥2​, which always has an answer.
How do you tell “no solution” from “infinitely many” without solving?
Compare two ranks. Build the augmented matrix [A∣b]. If rank([A∣b])>rank(A) then b has escaped the column space and there is no solution. If the two ranks are equal but smaller than the number of unknowns, you have free variables and an infinite family. Equal and full: exactly one.
An interviewer asks why anyone bothers with the column picture when the row picture is easier to draw.
Because ML lives in the column picture. Ax is a weighted sum of A’s columns, so solvability becomes “is b reachable from my features?” That one reframing hands you column space, rank, least squares as projection, and why collinear features destabilise a fit. The row picture stops being drawable past three dimensions; the column picture keeps working at ten thousand.

Say this back tomorrow

Ax=b · rows are constraints, columns are ingredients
  • One answer, no answer, or infinitely many. There is no fourth outcome.
  • Compare rank(A), rank([A∣b]) and n — that settles which case.
  • More rows than unknowns is the normal case: minimise the residual instead of demanding zero.

Unlocks

  • rank
  • column space
  • least squares
  • consistency
  • free variables
  • ridge regression

09foundation

Gaussian Elimination

Tidy the system into a staircase, then walk it back up.

Work down the rows. Subtract a copy of the first row from the rows underneath so their first entry becomes nothing, then repeat on the next column. None of this changes the answer, because subtracting one true rule from another true rule leaves a true rule. When you finish, the bottom row has a single unknown left in it, so you read that one off and feed it back up the staircase, one row at a time, until every unknown is known.

Like folding a road map down to one route. Every fold hides a panel you do not need. The roads never move, so the route you end up driving is the one that was always there — you have simply folded away everything that was making it hard to read.

Three row operations — swap two rows, scale a row by a nonzero, add a multiple of one row to another — leave the solution set untouched, because each one is reversible. Forward elimination drives A to upper-triangular U; back substitution then costs O(n2). The multipliers you used are not thrown away: they are L, and the whole procedure is the factorisation PA=LU, with P recording the row swaps. Total cost 32​n3 flops, and the factorisation is reusable across every right-hand side you meet later.

Partial pivoting — always move the largest-magnitude candidate into the pivot position — is not bureaucratic tidiness. A pivot near zero divides the rest of the row by something tiny and blows rounding error up with it; classic 2×2 examples lose every digit of accuracy without it. Push all the way to reduced row echelon form and the same machinery hands you the rank, a basis for the null space, and the inverse, though you should want none of those from row reduction on floating-point data.

You reach for it when

  • Solving a square system by hand, or explaining what solve actually does.
  • Finding rank, a null-space basis, or which constraints are redundant.
  • Reusing one factorisation across hundreds of right-hand sides.
  • Debugging a “singular matrix” error — elimination shows you which row went flat.

The trap

Pivoting is not optional. A pivot of 10−18 is arithmetically legal and numerically fatal, which is why every library does partial pivoting and returns P alongside L and U. The second trap: elimination reports exact rank, and in floating point exact zeros essentially never appear, so a rank read off row reduction of real data is really a guess about tolerance. Use the SVD for that.

The math about (2/3)n³ flops once · then O(n²) per solve

PA=LUAx=b⟹Ly=Pb,Ux=yfactorise once, and every extra right-hand side after that is two cheap substitutions

In NumPy / PyTorch

import scipy.linalg as sla
lu, piv = sla.lu_factor(A)          # the elimination itself: O(n^3), done once
x1 = sla.lu_solve((lu, piv), b1)    # each further solve is only O(n^2)
x2 = sla.lu_solve((lu, piv), b2)    # ...and the next 500 are nearly free

P, L, U = sla.lu(A)                 # P is the pivoting. it is why this is stable.
np.allclose(P @ L @ U, A)           # True
np.abs(np.diag(U)).min()            # tiny pivot = the matrix is nearly singular

Where this lives in real ML code

np.linalg.solve is not doing anything cleverer than this: it calls LAPACK gesv, which is getrf (LU by Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting) followed by getrs (the two substitutions). When a Gaussian process or a Kalman filter throws LinAlgError: Matrix is singular to machine precision, elimination has hit a pivot it cannot use. The standard fix is a small jitter on the diagonal; the standard mistake is making that jitter big enough to quietly change the model.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Why is it legal to subtract one row from another?
Because both rows are true statements about the same x. If r1​(x)=b1​ and r2​(x)=b2​ hold, then (r2​−αr1​)(x)=b2​−αb1​ holds too — and the step undoes itself by adding αr1​ back. Reversible means no solution can be created or destroyed, so the solution set is exactly what it was before.
One matrix, 500 different right-hand sides. What do you do?
Factorise once, substitute 500 times. PA=LU costs 32​n3; every solve after that is two triangular substitutions at O(n2). Re-running elimination per right-hand side is 500 times the work, and computing A−1 to reuse it is both slower and less accurate. If A is symmetric positive definite, use Cholesky and halve the cost again.
Elimination hands you a pivot of 0.0000000001 and does not raise. Now what?
Treat it as a red flag, not a number. Dividing by it scales existing rounding error by 1010, so the answer coming back can be noise wearing ten confident decimal places. Partial pivoting should have swapped a larger row in; if there was nothing larger, the matrix is effectively singular. Check np.linalg.cond(A), then regularise or drop the redundant column — do not just let it run.

Say this back tomorrow

forward elimination → U · back substitution → x · the multipliers are L
  • Swap, scale, add a multiple: three reversible moves that never touch the solution set.
  • Zeros go in under the diagonal, one column at a time, top-left to bottom-right.
  • It is LU underneath. Factorise once, then every new right-hand side is cheap.

Unlocks

  • LU decomposition
  • partial pivoting
  • row echelon form
  • back substitution
  • Cholesky
  • LAPACK getrf

10foundation

Determinants

One number: how much bigger did everything get?

Send a square through the matrix and it comes out as a slanted, resized version of itself. The determinant is the one number that says how many times bigger the area got. Three means three times the area. A half means it shrank. A negative number means the shape came out mirrored. And zero is the one that matters: the shape was squashed completely flat, so whatever used to be there is gone and no amount of cleverness brings it back.

Like the zoom dial on a photocopier. The determinant is that dial, reading in area rather than percent, with two settings the office copier hides from you: it can print the page mirrored, and it can be turned down until the copy comes out as a single black line with nothing left on it to read.

detA is the signed volume scale factor of the unit cube under A. The sign is orientation: positive keeps handedness, negative means a reflection got baked in. It is multiplicative, det(AB)=detAdetB, so det(A−1)=1/detA and det(A⊤)=detA; it equals the product of the eigenvalues, and for a triangular matrix the product of the diagonal. And detA=0 is the same sentence as: singular, rank deficient, non-trivial null space, a zero eigenvalue, no inverse.

Compute it through LU — the product of U’s diagonal times the sign of the row swaps, O(n3) — never by cofactor expansion, which is O(n!) and hopeless past about n=12. And do not use it as a health check: det(0.1I100​)=10−100, which underflows to zero on a matrix that is perfectly conditioned. For conditioning use κ or the smallest singular value; for likelihoods use slogdet, which returns the sign and log∣det∣ separately and never overflows.

You reach for it when

  • Asking whether a square matrix can be inverted at all.
  • Change of variables: the Jacobian determinant is the density correction factor.
  • Gaussian log-likelihoods, which always carry a log-determinant of the covariance.
  • Reasoning about whether a transform preserves volume or flips orientation.

The trap

A small determinant does not mean nearly singular. Scale a perfectly healthy 100×100 matrix by 0.1 and its determinant drops by 10−100 while its conditioning does not move at all. The determinant answers “is this exactly singular”, a yes/no question floating point cannot answer honestly anyway. For “how close to singular”, use np.linalg.cond or σmin​.

The math O(n³) through LU · never O(n!) by cofactors

det(AB)=detAdetBdetA=∏i​λi​detA=0⟺A−1 does not exist∣detA∣ is the volume scale · the sign is an orientation flip

In NumPy / PyTorch

A = np.array([[2., 1.], [0., 1.5]])
np.linalg.det(A)                # 3.0 -> areas triple

B = np.array([[1., 2.], [2., 4.]])   # row 2 is just 2x row 1
np.linalg.det(B)                # ~0.0 -> flat, singular, no inverse

sign, logdet = np.linalg.slogdet(cov)   # what a log-likelihood actually wants
np.linalg.det(0.1 * np.eye(100))    # 0.0 by underflow...
np.linalg.cond(0.1 * np.eye(100))   # ...but 1.0. det is not a health check.

Where this lives in real ML code

Normalizing flows are built on this: every layer has to report log∣detJ∣ of its Jacobian for each sample, which is why RealNVP and Glow use coupling layers and triangular maps whose determinant is a product down a diagonal instead of an O(n3) factorisation per sample. Closer to everyday code, the multivariate normal log-density carries a −21​logdetΣ term, which scipy.stats.multivariate_normal takes from an eigendecomposition — and which is why it refuses a singular covariance outright unless you pass allow_singular=True.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

What does a determinant of −2 tell you?
Two separate things at once. Areas double, and orientation flips — the transform contains a reflection, so a shape traced counterclockwise comes out clockwise. The magnitude is the scale factor, the sign is the handedness. In 3-D it means a right-handed frame comes back left-handed.
detA=0. List everything you now know.
These are all one fact wearing different hats. A is singular; it has no inverse; it is rank deficient; there is a nonzero v with Av=0; at least one eigenvalue is zero; at least one singular value is zero; the columns are linearly dependent. Geometrically it flattens space onto a lower-dimensional subspace, so the map is not one-to-one and there is nothing to undo it with.
Someone guards a production solver with if abs(det(A)) < 1e-10: raise. What breaks?
Both directions. A perfectly conditioned matrix that happens to be scaled small trips the alarm for nothing — det(10−3I10​)=10−30. And a badly conditioned matrix can have a determinant near 1 and sail straight through. Determinant scales like cn under A→cA; conditioning does not move at all. Guard on np.linalg.cond(A) or σmin​ instead.

Say this back tomorrow

∣detA∣ = volume scale · sign = flip · detA=0 = collapse
  • One number for the whole transform: what happened to area, or volume.
  • Zero means a dimension was destroyed. Singular, no inverse, information gone for good.
  • Multiplicative: det(AB)=detAdetB. Chain transforms, multiply their scale factors.

Unlocks

  • singular matrix
  • Jacobian determinant
  • orientation
  • slogdet
  • normalizing flows
  • volume scaling

11foundation

Matrix Inverse

The undo button, and why you rarely press it.

The inverse is the matrix that puts everything back exactly where it started. Send a point out through one matrix, bring it home through the inverse, and it lands on its original spot. It only exists if the first matrix flattened nothing, because once two different points have been squashed onto the same place, nothing can ever tell them apart again. And here is the part that surprises people: in real code you almost never build one.

Like working a recipe backwards. Building the inverse is writing out the full un-recipe for every cake that could ever come out of that oven. Nearly always you only care about the one cake sitting in front of you, and reasoning back from that single cake is both quicker and more accurate.

A−1 is the unique matrix with A−1A=AA−1=I. It exists exactly when A is square and non-singular: detA=0, full rank, trivial null space, no zero singular value. Order reverses through a product, (AB)−1=B−1A−1, and transpose commutes with it, (A⊤)−1=(A−1)⊤. For the friendly matrices you get it for nothing: Q−1=Q⊤ and diag(d)−1=diag(1/d). Existence is binary; usefulness is not, and that gap is where production code gets hurt.

To solve Ax=b use solve(A, b), never inv(A) @ b. Forming the inverse costs about 2n3 flops against 32​n3 for an LU solve — three times the work — and it is less accurate: the explicit inverse of an ill-conditioned matrix accumulates error in every one of its n2 entries, and then you multiply that error by b. A direct solve keeps a backward-error guarantee of roughly κ(A) times machine epsilon; routing through inv throws that away and buys nothing.

You reach for it when

  • On a whiteboard, where writing the inverse is simply the clearest notation.
  • You genuinely need every entry — a precision matrix, the inverse of a covariance, is a real case.
  • Tiny fixed matrices reused millions of times, like a 3-by-3 camera intrinsic.
  • Almost never otherwise. Reach for solve, lstsq, cho_solve or pinv.

The trap

The honest one: writing np.linalg.inv(A) @ b. It is roughly 3× the flops of np.linalg.solve(A, b) and it loses accuracy for free. The second trap is inv on a near-singular matrix — it does not raise, it hands back enormous numbers that look exactly like an answer. Check np.linalg.cond(A) first: if it reads 10k, you have already lost about k digits.

The math inv: about 2n³ flops · solve: about (2/3)n³

A−1A=AA−1=I(AB)−1=B−1A−1A−1 exists⟺detA=0solve the system you have; do not build the inverse you do not need

In NumPy / PyTorch

x = np.linalg.inv(A) @ b        # 3x the work and worse accuracy. do not.
x = np.linalg.solve(A, b)       # LU with partial pivoting. do this.

# symmetric positive definite (covariance, kernel, gram)? faster again:
c, low = sla.cho_factor(K + 1e-6 * np.eye(n))   # jitter keeps it factorable
x = sla.cho_solve((c, low), y)

np.linalg.cond(A)               # 1e12 -> about 12 digits already gone
np.linalg.pinv(A) @ b           # singular or non-square: least-squares answer

Where this lives in real ML code

Gaussian process regression is the standard cautionary tale. The textbook posterior mean is written K−1y, and nobody computes it that way: sklearn’s GaussianProcessRegressor Cholesky-factorises K+σ2I and calls cho_solve, while GPyTorch skips the factorisation entirely and runs conjugate gradients, because a kernel matrix built on close-together points is numerically singular. The same instinct shows up in linear regression: sklearn never forms (X⊤X)−1, it hands the problem to a QR or SVD least-squares driver.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

When does A−1 exist?
Square and non-singular — and every phrasing of that is the same fact. detA=0, full rank n, columns linearly independent, null space is only the zero vector, no zero eigenvalue, no zero singular value, the map is one-to-one and onto. Fail any one of those and you have failed all of them at once.
Code review: w = np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X) @ X.T @ y. What do you say?
Two problems, and the second is the serious one. First, use a solver: np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X, X.T @ y) is about 3× cheaper and more accurate. Second, X⊤X squares the condition number — κ(X⊤X)=κ(X)2 — so you have doubled the digits you lose before solving anything at all. The right answer is np.linalg.lstsq(X, y), which goes through QR or SVD and never forms the normal equations.
Explain out loud why a non-square matrix has no inverse.
Shapes first, then information. An (m,n) matrix maps n dimensions into m, and a true inverse would have to satisfy A−1A=In​ and AA−1=Im​ at once, which needs the two identities to be the same size. A tall matrix can have a left inverse and a wide one a right inverse, never both. When m<n the map has already thrown directions away: infinitely many inputs share an output, so there is nothing to return to. The pseudo-inverse picks one sensible answer rather than pretending.

Say this back tomorrow

A−1A=I · use solve(A,b), not inv(A) @ b
  • The undo exists only if nothing was flattened: detA=0, full rank, no zero singular value.
  • Order reverses: (AB)−1=B−1A−1. Free for orthogonal and diagonal matrices.
  • In production you solve the system in front of you. Building the inverse is 3× the work and less accurate.

Unlocks

  • np.linalg.solve
  • condition number
  • pseudo-inverse
  • Cholesky
  • normal equations
  • ridge regularisation

12core

Vector Spaces & Subspaces

A place where adding and stretching cannot kick you out.

A vector space is a room your arrows can never escape. Add two of them and you land back in the room. Stretch one to any size and you are still in the room. A subspace is a smaller room inside the big one that obeys the same rule. The test is short: it has to contain the zero point, and it has to survive adding and stretching. Fail either one and it is just a shape, not a subspace.

Like a LEGO set with only flat one-stud plates. Snap any of them together and the result is still flat. A flat layer lying on the table is a subspace; lift that same layer into the air and it stops being one, because the table — zero — is no longer part of it.

A vector space is a set closed under addition and scalar multiplication: if u,v∈V and a is a scalar, then au+v∈V. A subspace is a subset that is still closed, which forces exactly three things — it contains 0, it is closed under +, and it is closed under scaling. Every subspace of Rn is a point, a line, a plane or a higher flat sheet, and every one of them passes through the origin. Anything offset from the origin is an affine set, not a subspace — which is exactly why the bias term is stored apart from the weights.

This is not vocabulary for its own sake: the column space, the row space and the null space are all subspaces, and half of what you will say about a matrix is really a statement about which flat sheet its outputs are trapped on.

You reach for it when

  • Asking whether a set of solutions is a line, a plane, or nothing
  • Reasoning about column space, row space and null space — all three are subspaces
  • Explaining why a linear layer with no bias must send zero to zero
  • Deciding whether a cloud of embeddings can be treated as one flat sheet

The trap

Straight answer: this is the most abstract card on the page, so hold one concrete image and let the words hang off it — a subspace is a flat sheet pinned to the origin. The classic trap is a plane like z = 1. It is flat, it looks exactly like a plane, and it is not a subspace: multiply any point on it by 0 and you land at the origin, which is not on it.

The math one test, three consequences

V⊆Rn is a subspace when 0∈V, u+v∈V, and cu∈V for all u,v∈V and all scalars c. In practice you check one thing: is au+bv∈V for every a,b? That single closure test implies all three. Setting a=b=0 is what forces 0∈V.

In NumPy / PyTorch

import numpy as np
W = np.random.randn(4, 3)
b = np.random.randn(4)

print(W @ np.zeros(3))       # [0 0 0 0]  -> outputs form a subspace
print(W @ np.zeros(3) + b)   # b, not 0   -> affine, NOT a subspace

Where this lives in real ML code

A linear layer with no bias maps the origin to the origin, so its outputs are trapped in a subspace of the output dimension — the column space of W. Switch the bias on and you slide that whole sheet off the origin, which is why frameworks keep weight and bias as separate tensors and why weight decay is usually applied to the weights only. PCA is the same idea with teeth: it hunts for the best low-dimensional subspace through your data, and the mean-centring step exists precisely so that the sheet passes through zero.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Is the set of all vectors in R³ with z = 1 a subspace? Why or why not?
No. It fails on the very first check: it does not contain the origin, since (0,0,0) has z=0. It also fails closure — add two of its points and you get z=2. It is an affine plane, a subspace that has been shifted, and shifting is exactly what a bias term does.
Explain out loud, with no symbols, why every subspace has to contain the origin.
Because you are allowed to shrink. A subspace has to survive stretching by any amount, and zero is an amount. Take any arrow that lives in the subspace, shrink it all the way to nothing, and wherever you land has to be inside too. That landing point is the origin.
Your model outputs sit in R⁷⁶⁸ but you find they all lie on a 40-dimensional sheet that misses the origin. What is going on?
There is a constant offset — almost always a bias. The outputs are affine, not a subspace. Subtract the mean and the sheet slides back onto the origin, at which point it is a genuine 40-dimensional subspace and PCA, rank and null-space talk all become valid. This is why centring is step one of PCA, not an optional tidy-up.

Say this back tomorrow

closed under + and ×, and it always contains 0
  • A subspace is a flat sheet pinned to the origin.
  • Point, line, plane, hyperplane — there is nothing else it can be.
  • Miss the origin and it is affine, not a subspace. That is the bias term.

  • column space
  • null space
  • affine set
  • bias term
  • PCA centring

Span

Everywhere you can get to by mixing and stretching.

Take a few arrows. You are allowed to stretch each one, flip it backwards, and add the results together. The span is the complete list of places you can end up. One arrow gets you a line. Two arrows pointing genuinely different ways get you a whole flat plane. Two arrows pointing the same way still only get you a line, because the second one told you nothing you did not already know.

Like a paint set with two tubes. The span is every colour you can mix from those two, at any strength, in any ratio. Buy a third tube that is already a blend of the first two and your palette does not get one shade bigger.

The span of {v1​,…,vk​} is the set of all linear combinations c1​v1​+⋯+ck​vk​, and it is always a subspace because that set is closed by construction. Span is what a matrix–vector product actually computes: Ax is a weighted sum of the columns of A, so the set of reachable outputs is exactly span(columns of A), the column space. That gives you the solvability rule in one line: Ax=b has a solution if and only if b lies in that span.

Span is a set, not a number. Its size — the dimension of that set — is the rank. Adding a vector that already lies in the span lengthens your list of columns and changes nothing at all about what you can reach.

You reach for it when

  • Asking whether a linear system has any solution at all
  • Working out what a set of feature columns can actually express
  • Explaining what the column space of a weight matrix is
  • Checking whether a new feature adds information or just repeats one

The trap

Second most abstract card here, so pin it to one picture and move on: span is a reachable set — the colours you can mix from the tubes you own. The trap is counting vectors instead of counting directions. Ten vectors that all lie on the same line span a line, not anything ten-dimensional, and an eleventh copy still spans that same line.

The math a set, not a number

span(v1​,…,vk​)={c1​v1​+⋯+ck​vk​:ci​∈R} Ax=x1​a1​+⋯+xn​an​ over the columns ai​ of A, so the reachable set is Col(A)=span(a1​,…,an​) and Ax=b is solvable ⟺b∈Col(A).

In NumPy / PyTorch

import numpy as np
a = np.array([1., 2., 3.])
b = 2 * a                        # same direction, nothing new
M = np.stack([a, b], axis=1)      # 3 x 2 matrix, two columns

np.linalg.matrix_rank(M)     # 1  -> the span is a line, not a plane
np.linalg.matrix_rank(np.stack([a, a+b, b], 1))  # still 1

Where this lives in real ML code

The dummy-variable trap is a span bug. One-hot encode a categorical, keep every level and an intercept column, and that intercept is already in the span of the level columns — they sum to it. The design matrix stops being full rank, and your solver either raises LinAlgError or quietly returns one of infinitely many coefficient vectors. Vector search is the friendly version of the same question: a query is only answerable to the extent it lands near the span of what you actually indexed.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Three vectors in R³. Do they always span R³?
No. Only if they are linearly independent. Take (1,0,0), (2,0,0) and (0,1,0): three vectors, but the first two share a direction, so the span is just a plane. You need three independent directions, not three vectors.
Explain out loud what the column space of a weight matrix is, without using the word span.
It is every output the layer is capable of producing. The layer takes your input numbers and uses them as dials on its columns, adding the scaled columns together. So the outputs it can ever emit are exactly the sums you can build from those columns — nothing outside that set is reachable, no matter what you feed in.
You add a feature that is the sum of two features already in your design matrix. What happens to the span?
Nothing. The span is unchanged, because the new column was already reachable. What does change is that the matrix is now rank-deficient: you have one more column but not one more direction, so X⊤X becomes singular and the least-squares solution stops being unique.

Say this back tomorrow

span = every weighted sum you can build
  • Span is a reachable set, not a count of vectors.
  • One direction gives a line, two give a plane, k independent ones give k dimensions.
  • Ax=b is solvable exactly when b sits in the span of the columns.

Unlocks

  • column space
  • linear combination
  • rank
  • linear independence
  • dummy-variable trap

Linear Independence

Does every arrow earn its place, or is one a copy?

A set of arrows is independent when none of them can be built out of the others. Every arrow contributes a direction nobody else covers. They are dependent when one is just a stretched copy of another, or a sum of a few of them. Dependence is not an error, it is redundancy: you are paying for a direction you already had, and you can no longer tell which arrow deserves the credit.

Like a key ring where two keys open the same door. Nothing is broken and the door still opens, but one key is dead weight — and if someone asks which key got you in, you genuinely cannot say.

v1​,…,vk​ are linearly independent when c1​v1​+⋯+ck​vk​=0 forces every ci​=0: the only way to cancel them out is to use none of them. Dependence means some non-trivial combination hits zero, so the matrix holding them as columns has a null space bigger than {0}. Geometrically, k independent vectors bound a genuine k-dimensional volume and dependence squashes that volume to nothing. For a square matrix the whole chain collapses into one: independent columns ⟺det=0⟺ full rank ⟺ invertible.

In regression this is multicollinearity, and it is the interview answer. If two feature columns are perfectly correlated, X⊤X is singular and (X⊤X)−1 does not exist. If they are merely nearly correlated, X⊤X is near-singular: its smallest eigenvalue sits close to zero, so inverting it divides by something tiny and the fitted coefficients explode with wild signs and huge standard errors — while the predictions stay perfectly fine. Ridge fixes it by solving (X⊤X+λI)−1X⊤y, which lifts that smallest eigenvalue off the floor.

You reach for it when

  • Deciding whether a feature is redundant before you fit anything
  • Explaining why regression coefficients came out huge and unstable
  • Checking whether a square matrix can be inverted at all
  • Working out how many columns a design matrix really needs

The trap

The interview trap is treating near-dependence as fine because the code did not crash. np.linalg.solve only fails on exact singularity; at a correlation of 0.999 it returns numbers quite happily, and those numbers are garbage — resample a few rows and the coefficients flip sign. Check np.linalg.cond, not just whether it threw.

The math the only combination that kills them is the zero one

c1​v1​+⋯+ck​vk​=0⟹c1​=⋯=ck​=0 Square A: independent columns ⟺detA=0⟺rank(A)=n⟺A−1 exists. Near-dependence shows up as a large condition number κ=σmax​/σmin​. Rule of thumb only, not a law: above 103 start worrying, above 106 treat the coefficients as noise.

In NumPy / PyTorch

import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x1 = rng.normal(size=500)
x2 = x1 + 1e-3 * rng.normal(size=500)  # corr 0.999999, not identical
X  = np.column_stack([x1, x2])
y  = 3 * x1 + rng.normal(size=500)      # truth: [3, 0]

np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)[0]  # [ 33.8, -30.8 ]  -> nonsense
np.linalg.cond(X.T @ X)               # 4.6e6  -> near-singular
X @ np.array([33.8, -30.8])   # predictions are still fine!

Where this lives in real ML code

Ship a model with price, price_usd and log_price in the same design matrix and the RMSE will look perfectly healthy while the coefficients become fiction — retrain on a slightly different sample and the signs flip. Anyone reading a feature-importance table off that model is reading noise. The same failure shows up as duplicated one-hot levels, as a leaked target column, and in embeddings as near-duplicate dimensions; it is why people drop one level of every one-hot and why ridge exists.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Two of your features are correlated at 0.98 and the model still predicts well. Is anything actually wrong?
Yes, but not where people look. Predictions are fine — the span is barely affected, so the fitted surface is fine. What breaks is attribution: X⊤X is near-singular, coefficient variance is inflated, and the split of credit between the two features is arbitrary. If you only ever predict, ignore it. The moment you interpret a coefficient, it is a real bug.
Can four vectors in R³ ever be linearly independent?
Never. You cannot have more independent directions than dimensions, so any k>n vectors in Rn are dependent. Equivalently: a 3×4 matrix has rank at most 3, so by rank–nullity its null space has dimension at least 1 — there is guaranteed to be a non-zero combination that cancels out.
Say out loud, in one sentence to a non-technical stakeholder, why you dropped one of two near-duplicate features.
“The two columns say almost the same thing, so the model cannot tell which one is doing the work — it splits the credit between them at random and the numbers swing wildly between retrains. Dropping one costs us no accuracy and makes the explanation stable.” Note what you did not promise: better predictions. You promised stability and interpretability.

Say this back tomorrow

∑i​ci​vi​=0 only when every ci​=0
  • Independent means every vector adds a direction nobody else has.
  • Dependent columns make X⊤X singular and the coefficients explode.
  • More vectors than dimensions is always dependent. No exceptions.

Unlocks

  • multicollinearity
  • condition number
  • rank
  • determinant
  • ridge regression
  • VIF

Basis & Dimension

The smallest set of arrows that still reaches everything.

A basis is a set of arrows that is greedy enough and lean enough at the same time. Greedy: mixing them reaches every point in the space. Lean: not one of them is a copy of the others. Take one away and you lose places you could reach. Add one more and you gain nothing. Dimension is simply how many arrows a basis needs. Different bases describe the same point with different numbers, but they always need the same count.

Like the alphabet. Twenty-six letters, and every word in the language is some arrangement of them. Delete a letter and words go missing; invent a twenty-seventh that is just “th” glued together and you have not spelled a single new word.

A basis is a linearly independent spanning set. Independence kills redundancy, spanning guarantees coverage, and together they force uniqueness: every v has exactly one coordinate vector in that basis. Any two bases of the same space have the same number of vectors, and that number is the dimension. Changing basis is just a matrix — if B holds the new basis vectors as columns, then v=B[v]B​ and [v]B​=B−1v. The point never moves; only the numbers describing it do. Orthonormal bases are the ones worth wanting, because there B−1=B⊤.

Every decomposition later on this page is a hunt for a better basis. PCA looks for the basis where the coordinates are uncorrelated and front-loaded with variance; the eigenbasis is the one where a matrix stops mixing directions and merely scales them.

You reach for it when

  • Working out how many numbers a representation really needs
  • Reading a change-of-basis or rotation step in a paper
  • Understanding what PCA components actually are
  • Explaining why an embedding dimension is a design choice, not a fact

The trap

Coordinates are not the vector. [3, 2] means nothing until you say which basis, and the standard basis is a convention rather than a law of nature. Second trap, and interviewers do ask for it by name: a basis is minimal by definition, so “a basis with a redundant vector in it” is a contradiction — that thing is a spanning set.

The math unique coordinates, basis-independent count

v=c1​b1​+⋯+cn​bn​ with the ci​ unique, and dimV=n for every basis. Change of basis: [v]B​=B−1v and v=B[v]B​. If B is orthonormal then B−1=B⊤, so the round trip costs two matrix multiplies at O(n2) and no inversion at all — which is the entire reason rotations are cheap.

In NumPy / PyTorch

import numpy as np
B = np.array([[2., 1.], [1., 3.]])  # new basis, stored as COLUMNS
v = np.array([5., 5.])            # the point, in standard coords

c = np.linalg.solve(B, v)         # [2., 1.]  -> same point, new numbers
B @ c                             # [5., 5.]  -> and back again

Where this lives in real ML code

Every embedding table is a basis choice you did not make deliberately. The 768 numbers a text encoder hands you are coordinates in whatever basis training happened to land on, which is exactly why individual dimensions are uninterpretable while distances and angles between vectors are meaningful. PCA and SVD are basis changes that pick a better one: rotate until the first few coordinates carry most of the variance, keep those, drop the rest. A low-rank projection layer is doing the same trick with learned axes.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

What is the difference between a spanning set and a basis?
A basis is a spanning set with the fat trimmed off. Both reach every point. A spanning set is allowed to carry redundant vectors; a basis is additionally independent, which is what makes the coordinates unique. Drop the independence and a point has many valid coordinate vectors, and that ambiguity is precisely the multicollinearity problem.
Someone hands you a “basis for R⁵” containing six vectors. What went wrong?
It cannot be a basis. Six vectors in R5 are guaranteed to be dependent, so at least one is a combination of the others. It may well span R5 — then it is a spanning set, and you can throw one vector away to get down to an actual basis of five.
Explain out loud why the individual dimensions of a word embedding usually mean nothing.
Because the basis is arbitrary. Nothing in training pins the axes to human concepts — rotate the whole space and every distance, angle and dot product is unchanged, so the model is equally happy. Dimension 42 is a coordinate in one arbitrary rotation among infinitely many. That is also why interpretability work hunts for a new basis, as sparse autoencoders do, rather than reading the raw axes.

Say this back tomorrow

independent + spanning = basis; dim is how many
  • A basis is the smallest set that still reaches everything.
  • Coordinates depend on the basis. The dimension never does.
  • Orthonormal basis ⇒B−1=B⊤, and projection is just a dot product.

  • eigenbasis
  • PCA

  • dimension
