Rank

How many directions actually survive the matrix?

Rank counts the directions a matrix keeps. Push a square of space through it: if the square comes out as a tilted square, nothing was lost and the rank is full. If it comes out squashed flat onto a line, one direction died and the rank dropped. So rank measures how much real information the matrix carries. A huge table of numbers can still have tiny rank, which just means most of its columns are echoes of a few.

Like the shadow of your hand on a wall. The hand has three dimensions, the shadow has two, and no amount of squinting gets the third one back. Rank is how many dimensions the shadow still has after the light has done its work.

Rank is the dimension of the column space — the number of linearly independent columns — and the non-obvious theorem is that it equals the number of independent rows. Row rank = column rank, always, so rank(A)≤min(m,n). Full rank means you hit that bound; rank-deficient means you did not, and something collapsed. Rank–nullity stitches it together: rank(A)+nullity(A)=n, the number of columns. Numerically, rank is the count of non-zero singular values, and in floating point “non-zero” means “above a tolerance” — which is why matrix_rank takes a threshold.

Treat rank as an information budget and the applications fall out. A 4096×4096 weight update holds 16.7M parameters, but LoRA assumes the useful part of that update is low rank and stores it as BA with B∈R4096×r and A∈Rr×4096: at r=8 that is 65,536 numbers, about 256× fewer, and it works because fine-tuning nudges a handful of directions rather than rebuilding the map. The flip side is the thing that breaks: if your design matrix X is rank-deficient then X⊤X is singular, the normal equations have no unique solution, and least squares returns whichever of infinitely many answers the solver liked.

You reach for it when

  • Diagnosing why a least-squares fit has no unique answer
  • Choosing the rank r for a LoRA adapter
  • Deciding how many PCA components to keep
  • Checking whether a wide feature table is secretly very small

The trap

Rank in floating point is a judgement call, not a fact: a matrix that is mathematically rank 2 shows singular values like 6e-16, and np.linalg.matrix_rank only calls it 2 because of its default tolerance. The bigger interview trap runs the other way — rank tells you nothing about magnitude or usefulness. A rank-1 matrix can be enormous, and a technically full-rank matrix can be numerically useless when its smallest singular value is a whisker above zero. For that question you want the condition number, not the rank.

The math rank≤min(m,n); SVD costs O(mnmin(m,n))

rank(A)=dimCol(A)=dimRow(A)=#{σi​>0} Rank–nullity: rank(A)+nullity(A)=n (columns). Full rank means rank=min(m,n). Rank-deficient X⇒X⊤X singular ⇒ no unique least-squares solution. Best rank-k approximation: keep the top k singular values (Eckart–Young).

In NumPy / PyTorch

import numpy as np
A = np.array([[1., 2., 3.],
              [2., 4., 6.],   # row 2 = 2 x row 1
              [1., 1., 1.]])

np.linalg.matrix_rank(A)              # 2  -> one direction died
np.linalg.svd(A, compute_uv=False)     # [8.52, 0.643, 6.2e-16]
#                                        that last one IS the collapse

# LoRA: a 4096x4096 update stored as B @ A with r = 8
2 * 4096 * 8, 4096 * 4096            # 65,536 vs 16,777,216  -> 256x fewer

Where this lives in real ML code

LoRA is the headline case: rather than updating a 4096×4096 weight matrix you learn a rank-8 correction and train a fraction of a percent of the parameters. Recommender systems are the older version — a user×item matrix with millions of entries gets modelled at rank 50, because taste genuinely is low-dimensional. And the thing that breaks in production: a design matrix with a duplicated or one-hot-redundant column is rank-deficient, so X.T @ X is singular, np.linalg.inv raises or returns nonsense, and lstsq silently hands you the minimum-norm answer out of infinitely many.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Why is row rank always equal to column rank, and what does that actually buy you?
Because both count the same thing: the dimension of the space the matrix maps onto. Row reduction preserves both, and the number of pivots is shared. What it buys you is freedom of attack — for a 10,000×5 matrix you never inspect ten thousand rows, because rank is at most 5, so you reason about the five columns instead. It also means rank(A)=rank(A⊤) for free.
A 10,000 x 500 matrix turns out to have rank 12. What does that tell you about the data?
That 488 of your 500 columns carry no new information. Everything lives on a 12-dimensional sheet, so twelve well-chosen features (or twelve PCA components) reproduce the whole table. Practically: compress it, expect near-zero reconstruction error, and be suspicious — that much redundancy usually means duplicated feature engineering or a leak.
Your least-squares solve returns different coefficients on every rerun with identical data. First thing you check?
Rank. Call np.linalg.matrix_rank(X) and compare it to the number of columns. If it is short, X is rank-deficient, X⊤X is singular, and there are infinitely many coefficient vectors giving the identical fit — the solver is picking among them, so tiny numerical differences change the answer. Fix the columns or add ridge; do not chase the seed.

Say this back tomorrow

rank+nullity=n  ·  row rank = column rank
  • Rank = how many directions survive = how much real information is in there.
  • Rank-deficient means collapsed space, which means no unique least-squares answer.
  • Low rank is the whole premise behind LoRA, PCA and matrix factorisation.

  • LoRA
  • condition number

  • PCA
  • matrix factorisation

Null Space

Everything the matrix crushes down to zero.

Some inputs go into a matrix and come out as nothing at all — a plain zero. The null space is the whole collection of those inputs. If only the zero input lands on zero, nothing is being lost and the matrix can be undone. If a whole line of inputs lands on zero, that line is information you can never get back, and any answer the matrix gives you can be slid along that line without changing a thing.

Like a shredder. Feed it a contract or feed it a blank page and you get the same pile of confetti out. The null space is every sheet that produces that identical pile — and the reason you cannot reverse the machine.

The null space, or kernel, is N(A)={x:Ax=0}, and it is always a subspace: it contains 0 and it is closed. Its dimension is the nullity, and rank–nullity says rank(A)+nullity(A)=n, the number of columns, not rows. Nullity 0 means the columns are independent and the map is injective. Nullity >0 means Ax=b has either no solution or infinitely many — because if x0​ works then so does x0​+z for every z∈N(A), so the solution set is a shifted copy of the null space.

The left null space {y:A⊤y=0} is the fourth of the four fundamental subspaces and lives on the output side. It is the orthogonal complement of the column space, which is exactly where least-squares residuals end up — the part of b that A can never reach, no matter which x you choose.

You reach for it when

  • Explaining why a linear system has infinitely many solutions
  • Working out what a rank-deficient design matrix is costing you
  • Reading the four fundamental subspaces in a textbook or a paper
  • Deciding which directions a projection or a pruning step throws away

The trap

Rank–nullity counts columns, not rows. For a 3×5 matrix the nullity is 5−rank, so it is at least 2 no matter what the numbers are: a wide matrix always has a non-trivial null space and therefore never has a unique solution. Second trap: a big null space does not make a system unsolvable. It makes it under-determined, which is quietly worse, because the solver returns one answer and never warns you.

The math rank + nullity = columns

N(A)={x∈Rn:Ax=0},    rank(A)+dimN(A)=n If Ax0​=b then the complete solution set is {x0​+z:z∈N(A)} — one particular answer plus the entire null space. Nullity 0⟺ columns independent ⟺ injective. For a wide matrix (m<n), nullity ≥n−m>0, always.

In NumPy / PyTorch

import numpy as np
from scipy.linalg import null_space

A = np.array([[1., 2., 3.],
              [2., 4., 6.]])   # rank 1, three columns

Z = null_space(A)          # shape (3, 2)  -> nullity = 3 - 1 = 2
A @ Z                      # ~0 : every column of Z is crushed

b  = np.array([6., 12.])
x0 = np.linalg.lstsq(A, b, rcond=None)[0]
A @ (x0 + 3.0 * Z[:, 0])  # [6., 12.] : still a solution. Infinitely many.

Where this lives in real ML code

This is why a rank-deficient design matrix is dangerous rather than merely broken. Add a redundant one-hot level and the null space stops being trivial, so the coefficient vector can slide freely along it: two training runs produce completely different coefficients that make byte-identical predictions, and any feature-importance story told about them is fiction. Pruning and quantisation exploit the same fact from the other side — directions the weights barely use sit close to the null space, so deleting them costs almost nothing.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

A matrix is 3 x 7. What is the smallest its null space can possibly be?
Dimension 4. Rank is capped at min(3,7)=3, and rank–nullity counts columns: nullity=7−rank≥7−3=4. This is the whole trap — people subtract from 3. Any wide system has a guaranteed non-trivial null space, so it can never have a unique solution.
Explain out loud why a non-trivial null space means infinitely many solutions.
Because you can always add a ghost. Suppose x0​ solves Ax=b, and z is a non-zero vector the matrix crushes to nothing. Then A(x0​+z)=Ax0​+Az=b+0=b, so x0​+z solves it too — and so does x0​+100z, and every other multiple. One solution plus a whole null space is infinitely many solutions.
Two runs of your regression give totally different coefficients but identical predictions. What does that say about the null space?
That it is non-trivial, so the design matrix is rank-deficient. The two coefficient vectors differ by something in N(X), which X maps to zero, so Xβ is the same both times. Look for a duplicated column, a redundant one-hot level, or a feature that is the sum of two others. Fix the columns, or add ridge, which makes the answer unique by penalising the null-space part to zero.

Say this back tomorrow

rank+nullity=n  (columns)
  • The null space is everything the matrix crushes to zero.
  • Nullity 0→ a unique answer. Nullity >0→ infinitely many.
  • Solution set = one particular answer + the whole null space.

  • rank-nullity
  • kernel
  • four fundamental subspaces
  • underdetermined system
  • least squares
  • pruning
  • ridge regression

Linear Transformations

A matrix is not a table. It is a verb.

Stop reading a matrix as a box of numbers and start reading it as a machine that moves space. Feed it any point, it hands you back a new point. Every grid line stays straight, stays evenly spaced, and the origin never budges. That is the whole rule. And here is the trick worth memorising: look at where the two little arrows along the axes land. Those two landing spots are literally the columns of the matrix.

Like a photograph of a room. The camera sends every point in the scene to some point on the film, and straight edges come out straight. Once you know where the corners of the room landed, you know where everything else landed too.

A matrix A∈Rm×n is a linear map T(x)=Ax. It obeys T(u+v)=T(u)+T(v) and T(cu)=cT(u), which is exactly why grid lines stay parallel and evenly spaced and why T(0)=0. The columns are not bookkeeping: Aej​ is literally column j, so A is completely determined by where the standard basis lands. Composing two maps is matrix multiplication, which is why AB means “do B, then A”, and why the product is associative but not commutative.

Anything that bends a grid line or shifts the origin is not linear. A layer computing Wx+b is affine, not linear — frameworks either carry b as a separate tensor or fold it into a homogeneous coordinate. Two scalars read off the map itself: detA is the volume scale factor, and rank(A) is the dimension of what is left after the map runs.

You reach for it when

  • You want to know what a layer does, not just its shape.
  • Reasoning about a rotation, scaling, shear or reflection.
  • Reading a weight matrix column by column instead of cell by cell.
  • Two operations in a row have to collapse into one.

The trap

The classic: AB is not BA. Rotate-then-scale is a different map from scale-then-rotate unless the scale is uniform. The other one interviewers actually ask: Wx + b is affine, not linear, because it moves the origin. Say “affine” unprompted and you sound like you have thought about it.

The math cost: O(mn) per vector, O(mnk) for a batch of k

T(x)=Ax, with A(αu+βv)=αAu+βAv and T(0)=0.   Column j of A is Aej​ — where the j-th basis vector lands.   Composition: (AB)x=A(Bx), so AB means “B first”.   detA is the volume scale factor; detA=0 means the map squashes space flat.

In NumPy / PyTorch

import numpy as np
A = np.array([[1., 1.], [0., 1.]])   # a shear
I = np.eye(2)
A @ I[:, 0]      # -> [1., 0.]   where i lands = column 0
A @ I[:, 1]      # -> [1., 1.]   where j lands = column 1

# composition is a product, read right to left
R = np.array([[0., -1.], [1., 0.]])  # 90-degree rotation
np.allclose(A @ R, R @ A)   # -> False. Order matters.

Where this lives in real ML code

Every nn.Linear(768, 3072) in a transformer MLP is one of these maps. Its weight is a 3072×768 matrix, and each of its 768 columns is where one input basis direction gets sent — which is what people are pointing at when they talk about a “direction in activation space”. Rotary position embedding is a literal rotation matrix applied to Q and K, and it works precisely because rotations are linear and leave dot products alone.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

A layer computes Wx + b. Is that a linear transformation? Say it out loud.
No — it is affine. Linearity demands T(0)=0, and W⋅0+b=b=0 whenever b=0. It becomes linear again if you append a 1 to x and fold b into an extra column of W (homogeneous coordinates). Volunteering the word “affine” is a cheap win in an interview.
Without multiplying anything: where does (0, 1) land under A = [[2, 3], [0, 4]]?
At (3,4) — the second column. Ae2​ is column 2 by definition. That is the entire memory hook: the columns are the images of the basis vectors, so you can read a small matrix’s behaviour straight off the page without touching arithmetic.
Why is matrix multiplication associative but not commutative?
Because it is function composition. Composition is associative — (f∘g)∘h=f∘(g∘h) — but doing g then f is a different function from f then g. Rotate-then-shear is visibly not shear-then-rotate; a sketch of a grid settles it faster than algebra.

Say this back tomorrow

A matrix is a function. Its columns are where the basis vectors land.
  • Straight stays straight, evenly spaced stays evenly spaced, the origin never moves.
  • Aej​ = column j. Read a small matrix by reading its columns.
  • AB means “do B first”. Associative, never commutative.

  • change of basis
  • affine layers

Orthogonality & Projections

The closest point, and the bit left over.

Two directions are orthogonal when they tell you nothing about each other — their agreement score is zero. Projection is the other half of the same idea. Given a direction, you split a vector into the part that lies along it and the part that does not. The along part is the closest you can possibly get. The leftover part sits at a perfect right angle to the direction, and that right angle is precisely why nothing closer exists.

Like your shadow on the ground at midday. The sun is straight overhead, so the shadow is the flattest, closest copy of you the ground can hold, and your height is the part the ground simply cannot show.

u⊥v exactly when u⊤v=0. The projection of v onto u is p=u⊤uu⊤v​u, and the residual r=v−p satisfies u⊤r=0 by construction. That orthogonality is not a bonus — it is the optimality condition, since p is the unique minimiser of ∥v−cu∥2​ over all scalars c. Onto a subspace with orthonormal basis Q, the projector is P=QQ⊤: symmetric and idempotent, P2=P. Pythagoras drops out: ∥v∥2=∥p∥2+∥r∥2.

Orthonormal matrices (Q⊤Q=I) are the ones numerical people reach for, because ∥Qx∥2​=∥x∥2​ means κ2​(Q)=1 and rounding error passes through unamplified. That is the whole reason QR and the SVD are built out of them, and why Householder reflections quietly replaced classical Gram–Schmidt in every serious library.

You reach for it when

  • Splitting a signal into a part you keep and a part you throw away.
  • Removing a known direction from an embedding.
  • Anything phrased as best approximation inside a subspace.
  • Checking whether two features carry the same information.

The trap

A zero dot product means uncorrelated only if both vectors are already mean-centred. Raw non-negative data — counts, TF-IDF, ReLU activations — almost never has orthogonal columns, so people read cosine similarity as correlation and get burned. Second: P = QQ^T holds only when Q has orthonormal columns; otherwise the projector is A(A^T A)^-1 A^T.

The math cost: O(n) onto one vector, O(nk) onto a k-dimensional subspace

p=u⊤uu⊤v​u,   r=v−p,   u⊤r=0.   Onto a subspace: P=A(A⊤A)−1A⊤, or simply QQ⊤ when Q is orthonormal.   P=P⊤=P2,   and ∥v∥22​=∥p∥22​+∥r∥22​.

In NumPy / PyTorch

u = np.array([3., 4.]); v = np.array([5., 1.])
p = (u @ v) / (u @ u) * u    # the projection of v onto u
r = v - p                    # the residual
u @ r                        # -> ~0.0   perpendicular, always

# projecting onto a whole subspace, the stable way
Q, _ = np.linalg.qr(A)       # orthonormal basis for col(A)
P = Q @ Q.T                  # never hand-roll A(A^T A)^-1 A^T
np.allclose(P @ P, P)        # -> True. Projecting twice changes nothing.

Where this lives in real ML code

Every time somebody “removes the gender direction” from a word embedding, or subtracts the top principal component from a batch of activations to kill a dominant nuisance signal, they are applying I - qq^T. Attention scores are dot products, and the fact that random vectors in high dimensions are very nearly orthogonal is the reason random projection and the LSH indexes inside FAISS work at all.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Prove in one line that the residual is perpendicular to u.
Substitute and watch it cancel. u⊤r=u⊤(v−u⊤uu⊤v​u)=u⊤v−u⊤uu⊤v​(u⊤u)=0. The scale factor was chosen precisely to make this vanish, which is why p is the closest point: any other coefficient leaves a component along u still on the table.
Interview trap: two features have dot product zero. Are they independent?
No. Orthogonal is not independent, and it is not even uncorrelated unless both are mean-centred. On a sample symmetric about zero, x and x2 are orthogonal yet perfectly dependent. Orthogonality is a geometric statement about one inner product; independence is a statement about a joint distribution.
Why do numerical libraries build everything out of orthonormal matrices?
Because they never amplify error. ∥Qx∥2​=∥x∥2​, so κ2​(Q)=1 and rounding error passes through unmagnified. That is why QR and SVD sit under least squares, and why a QR solve replaces (A⊤A)−1A⊤ in anything you would ship.

Say this back tomorrow

Project = keep the part along the direction. The leftover is always perpendicular.
  • p=u⊤uu⊤v​u; the residual is orthogonal by construction, which is what makes p closest.
  • P=QQ⊤ is symmetric and idempotent — projecting twice does nothing new.
  • Orthogonal is geometry, not statistics. It is not independence.

  • orthonormal basis
  • QR decomposition
  • Gram-Schmidt
  • least squares
  • cosine similarity

Least Squares

No exact answer exists, so take the closest one.

You have far more equations than unknowns, so no line goes through every point. Least squares picks the line that makes the total of the squared misses as small as it can be. Geometrically it is a projection: the target is out of reach, so you land on the nearest point you can actually reach. Squaring is what makes one big miss hurt more than several small ones.

Like six people picking one meeting time. No slot suits everybody, so you take the slot where the total inconvenience, counted harshly, is smallest — and everyone stays a little unhappy in a way nobody can fix.

An overdetermined system Xb≈y has no exact solution because y∈/col(X). Least squares minimises ∥y−Xb∥22​; setting the gradient to zero gives the normal equations X⊤Xb=X⊤y. Read them geometrically instead of algebraically: X⊤(y−Xb)=0 says the residual is orthogonal to every column of X, so Xb is the projection of y onto col(X). With full column rank the answer is unique, b=(X⊤X)−1X⊤y.

Then do not solve it that way. Forming X⊤X squares the condition number — κ2​(X⊤X)=κ2​(X)2 — so a merely awkward design matrix becomes numerically hopeless and you lose roughly twice as many digits. Use QR (X=QR⇒Rb=Q⊤y) or the SVD, which is exactly what np.linalg.lstsq does. Ridge, (X⊤X+λI)−1X⊤y, improves conditioning too, at the price of bias.

You reach for it when

  • More rows than columns, and no exact solution exists.
  • Fitting a regression, a calibration curve or a trend line.
  • Any problem phrased as minimise the sum of squared errors.
  • Solving for weights when the design matrix is tall and skinny.

The trap

Two of them. First, the residual is vertical, not perpendicular to the line — if the error lives in both variables you want total least squares instead. Second, nobody in production forms X.T @ X: it squares the condition number, so reach for np.linalg.lstsq (SVD-based) or a QR solve on X directly.

The math cost: QR is O(nd^2) for n rows and d features; normal equations are O(nd^2 + d^3) and far less stable

Minimise ∥y−Xb∥22​  ⇒  X⊤Xb=X⊤y  (the normal equations).   Full column rank: b=(X⊤X)−1X⊤y=X+y.   In practice X=QR⇒Rb=Q⊤y, or go through the SVD.   Conditioning: κ2​(X⊤X)=κ2​(X)2.

In NumPy / PyTorch

b, res, rank, sv = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)  # SVD-based. Do this.

# the textbook route, for understanding only
b_bad = np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X) @ X.T @ y   # squares the condition number

# the stable hand-rolled version
Q, R = np.linalg.qr(X)
b_qr = scipy.linalg.solve_triangular(R, Q.T @ y)

np.linalg.cond(X), np.linalg.cond(X.T @ X)   # -> c,  roughly c**2

Where this lives in real ML code

sklearn.linear_model.LinearRegression calls scipy.linalg.lstsq rather than inverting anything. This is also what quietly breaks when two features in a design matrix are near-duplicates: the fit still returns, but the coefficients swing wildly between retrains because X.T @ X is nearly singular. That is the “unstable coefficients” complaint people fix with ridge.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Derive the normal equations from geometry, not calculus.
The residual must be orthogonal to the column space. If y−Xb had any component inside col(X), you could shrink the error by nudging b. So X⊤(y−Xb)=0, which rearranges to X⊤Xb=X⊤y. Identical to differentiating, but you can say it in one breath at a whiteboard.
Interview trap: why should you never solve least squares with the normal equations?
Because κ2​(X⊤X)=κ2​(X)2. Forming the product squares the condition number, costing you roughly twice as many digits. A design matrix with κ2​=108 — utterly unremarkable — becomes 1016, right at the edge of double precision. QR and SVD work on X directly and never square anything.
What happens when X has two perfectly collinear columns?
X⊤X is singular and b is not unique — a whole line of coefficient vectors gives the identical fit. lstsq still returns something: the SVD picks the minimum-norm member via the pseudo-inverse. Ridge picks a different unique answer by adding λI before inverting.

Say this back tomorrow

Least squares is a projection. The residual is perpendicular to every column of X.
  • Normal equations X⊤Xb=X⊤y are just “residual ⊥ columns”.
  • Never form X⊤X: it squares the condition number. QR or SVD instead.
  • Rank-deficient means the answer is a set; the SVD hands you its shortest member.

Unlocks

  • linear regression
  • QR decomposition
  • condition number
  • ridge regression
  • pseudo-inverse

Trace & Frobenius Norm

Two ways to squeeze a whole matrix into one number.

Trace adds up the numbers running down the main diagonal, top left to bottom right. That one number does not change if you view the same matrix from a different set of axes, which is why people trust it. The Frobenius norm answers a different question: square every single cell, add them all, take the square root. It is just the ordinary length of the matrix, as if you had unrolled the whole grid into one long list.

Like the total row at the bottom of a spreadsheet. Nobody reads three hundred cells; they read one number that stands in for the sheet. Which number you pick depends on whether you care about the centre line or about the size of everything at once.

tr(A)=∑i​Aii​=∑i​λi​, and it is invariant under cyclic permutation, tr(ABC)=tr(BCA), hence invariant under change of basis, tr(P−1AP)=tr(A). The Frobenius norm is ∥A∥F​=∑ij​Aij2​​=tr(A⊤A)​=∑i​σi2​​ — the Euclidean norm of the flattened matrix, and also the ℓ2​ norm of its singular values. Those identities hand you spectral information from a sum you can compute in one pass.

Weight decay on a weight matrix is a λ∥W∥F2​ penalty whose gradient is 2λW — that is all L2 regularisation is. “How far apart are these two matrices?” almost always means ∥A−B∥F​, and Eckart–Young says truncated SVD is the best possible rank-k approximation in exactly that norm. Do not confuse it with the spectral norm ∥A∥2​=σ1​; they agree only when A has rank one.

You reach for it when

  • You need one scalar that says how big a matrix is.
  • Measuring the gap between two weight matrices or two embeddings.
  • Writing an L2 penalty over a whole weight tensor.
  • Simplifying an expression by rotating terms inside a trace.

The trap

tr(AB) = tr(BA) is true, but tr(ABC) = tr(ACB) is false — only cyclic rotations are allowed, not arbitrary reordering. And the Frobenius norm is not the spectral norm: ||A||_F is the L2 norm of all singular values, ||A||_2 only the largest. They can differ by a factor of the square root of the rank.

The math cost: trace is O(n) if you never form the product; Frobenius is O(mn), one pass

tr(A)=∑i​Aii​=∑i​λi​,   tr(ABC)=tr(BCA),   tr(P−1AP)=tr(A).   ∥A∥F2​=∑ij​Aij2​=tr(A⊤A)=∑i​σi2​.   And ∥A∥2​=σ1​≤∥A∥F​≤r​∥A∥2​ for rank r.

In NumPy / PyTorch

A = np.random.randn(4, 4)
np.trace(A), np.linalg.eigvals(A).sum().real        # -> equal
np.linalg.norm(A, 'fro'), np.sqrt(np.trace(A.T @ A))   # -> equal
np.linalg.norm(A, 'fro'), np.linalg.norm(A.ravel())    # -> equal too

# tr(A @ B) without ever building A @ B
np.einsum('ij,ji->', A, B)   # O(n*m) instead of O(n*m*n)

Where this lives in real ML code

The weight_decay knob in AdamW is a Frobenius penalty on every weight matrix; the gradient it adds is just a scaled copy of the weights. When you compare a quantised checkpoint against the FP16 original, the number people quote is torch.linalg.norm(W - W_q, 'fro') over ||W||_F. And the claim that a LoRA fine-tune is “low rank” is measured by how much of ||W||_F^2 sits in the top handful of singular values.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Why is the trace the same in any basis? Explain it out loud.
Because trace is cyclic. A change of basis sends A↦P−1AP, and tr(P−1AP)=tr(APP−1)=tr(A). That is also why it equals ∑i​λi​: eigenvalues are basis-independent, and in the eigenbasis the diagonal is the list of eigenvalues.
You need tr(AB) where A is 10000 x 5 and B is 5 x 10000. What do you do?
Compute tr(BA) instead. BA is 5×5; AB is 10000×10000 and would not fit in memory. Cyclic invariance turns a blow-up into a trivial product. Better still, np.einsum('ij,ji->', A, B) never forms either product at all.
Interview trap: is the Frobenius norm the same as the spectral norm?
No. ∥A∥F​=∑i​σi2​​ counts every singular value; ∥A∥2​=σ1​ counts only the largest. They coincide only for rank-one matrices, and it matters which you mean: Lipschitz bounds and gradient-explosion arguments need ∥A∥2​, while regularisation and approximation error use ∥A∥F​.

Say this back tomorrow

Trace = sum of the diagonal = sum of the eigenvalues. Frobenius = length of the flattened matrix.
  • tr(ABC)=tr(BCA) — cyclic only, and that is what makes trace basis-free.
  • ∥A∥F2​=tr(A⊤A)=∑i​σi2​. Weight decay is exactly this penalty.
  • ∥A∥2​=σ1​ is a different norm. Do not swap them under pressure.

Unlocks

  • eigenvalues
  • singular values
  • weight decay
  • Eckart-Young
  • matrix norms

Covariance & Gram Matrices

Multiply the data by itself, two different ways.

Take your data table: rows are samples, columns are features. Multiply it by its own flipped copy and you get a square summary. Do it one way round and the square is feature by feature — how much each pair of columns moves together. Do it the other way round and the square is sample by sample — how similar each pair of rows is. Same data, two squares, wildly different sizes.

Like a handful of darts in a board. Nobody cares where each dart went; you care about the pattern — how wide the spread is left to right, how wide up and down, and whether it leans. A covariance matrix is that pattern written down as numbers.

For X∈Rn×d: X⊤X is d×d, the Gram or scatter matrix, one entry per pair of features. XX⊤ is n×n, the kernel matrix, one entry per pair of samples. Covariance is the mean-centred, scaled version, Σ=n−11​Xc⊤​Xc​ with Xc​=X−xˉ. Both products are symmetric and positive semi-definite, because v⊤X⊤Xv=∥Xv∥22​≥0. If X=USV⊤ then X⊤X=VS2V⊤ and XX⊤=US2U⊤: same non-zero eigenvalues σi2​.

That PSD fact is the licence for the whole tier above this card. The spectral theorem gives a real symmetric matrix real eigenvalues and an orthogonal eigenbasis; positive semi-definiteness forces those eigenvalues to be ≥0. So PCA’s “variance explained” is never negative and its components are never oblique. When d≪n you work with X⊤X; when n≪d, or under the kernel trick, you work with XX⊤ and get the same spectrum. Eigenvalues, SVD and PCA next — all three are this one fact cashed out.

You reach for it when

  • Before PCA, whitening, or any variance-based dimensionality cut.
  • Checking whether two features are near-duplicates.
  • Kernel methods, where you only ever touch sample-by-sample similarity.
  • Diagnosing why a linear solve came back unstable.

The trap

X.T @ X is not the covariance matrix unless you centred first. Skip the mean subtraction and the top eigenvector simply points at where the data cloud sits, so your first principal component means nothing. Second trap: picking the wrong side. With two million samples and three hundred features, X @ X.T is a two-million-square matrix you cannot allocate.

The math cost: X^T X is O(n d^2), X X^T is O(n^2 d) — always form the small side

G=X⊤X∈Rd×d (features),   K=XX⊤∈Rn×n (samples).   Σ=n−11​Xc⊤​Xc​ with Xc​ mean-centred.   PSD: v⊤X⊤Xv=∥Xv∥22​≥0.   From X=USV⊤: G=VS2V⊤, K=US2U⊤ — same non-zero eigenvalues σi2​.

In NumPy / PyTorch

X = np.random.randn(1000, 20)   # n=1000 samples, d=20 features
Xc = X - X.mean(axis=0)      # CENTRE FIRST. always.
C  = (Xc.T @ Xc) / (len(X) - 1)  # (20, 20) covariance
np.allclose(C, np.cov(X, rowvar=False))   # -> True

G = X.T @ X    # (20, 20)     gram / scatter -> cheap
K = X @ X.T    # (1000, 1000) kernel         -> quadratic in n
np.allclose(np.linalg.eigvalsh(G)[-5:],
            np.linalg.eigvalsh(K)[-5:])   # -> True. Same spectrum.

Where this lives in real ML code

sklearn.decomposition.PCA never builds the covariance matrix — it centres X and runs an SVD, because that is the same eigendecomposition without the conditioning penalty. Gaussian process and kernel-SVM libraries live on the other side: they build the n-by-n kernel matrix and Cholesky it, which is why GPs fall over somewhere past ten thousand samples. Those "matrix is not positive definite" errors out of scipy.linalg.cholesky are this matrix losing rank to duplicate features or floating-point drift.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Why are PCA’s eigenvalues always real and non-negative?
Because the covariance matrix is real symmetric and positive semi-definite. Symmetry gives real eigenvalues and an orthogonal eigenbasis (spectral theorem); PSD follows from v⊤Xc⊤​Xc​v=∥Xc​v∥22​≥0, which forces λ≥0. Each eigenvalue is a variance, and a variance cannot be negative.
You have 2 million rows and 300 features. Which product do you form?
X⊤X, the 300×300 one. XX⊤ would be 2M×2M — roughly 32 terabytes in float64. They share the same non-zero eigenvalues, so you lose nothing. The rule: form the product on the small dimension, or skip both and take the SVD of X directly.
Interview trap: is X-transpose-X the covariance matrix?
Only after centring, and only up to a scale factor. X⊤X is the uncentred scatter matrix; Σ=n−11​Xc⊤​Xc​. Forget the mean subtraction and the dominant eigenvector aligns with the data’s mean direction, so your first principal component reports “where the cloud sits” rather than how it varies.

Say this back tomorrow

X⊤X is feature-by-feature and small. XX⊤ is sample-by-sample and huge. Both are symmetric PSD.
  • Covariance is the centred, scaled version: Σ=n−11​Xc⊤​Xc​. Centre first or PCA lies.
  • PSD because v⊤X⊤Xv=∥Xv∥22​≥0 — that is why eigenvalues are real and ≥0.
  • Both share the non-zero eigenvalues σi2​, so pick the cheap side. Everything in Advanced starts here.

Unlocks

  • PCA
  • spectral theorem
  • positive semi-definite
  • kernel trick
  • SVD
  • whitening

The Pseudo-inverse

What you use when the inverse does not exist.

Most matrices cannot be undone. They are the wrong shape, or they squash information flat, so there is no way back. The pseudo-inverse is the best available stand-in: it gets you as close to undoing the matrix as anything can. Give it too many equations and it returns the best compromise. Give it too few and it returns the smallest answer that fits. And for a matrix that genuinely has an inverse, it simply is the inverse.

Like translating a poem into another language and back again. You will not get your original words. You get the closest thing the round trip can produce — and if what you started with was simple enough, you get it back exactly.

From the SVD A=UΣV⊤, the Moore–Penrose pseudo-inverse is A+=VΣ+U⊤, where Σ+ transposes Σ and inverts every non-zero singular value, leaving the zeros as zeros. Overdetermined with full column rank: A+b is the least-squares solution, equal to (A⊤A)−1A⊤b. Underdetermined: A+b is the minimum-norm solution among infinitely many exact ones. Rank-deficient: it is both at once. And if A is invertible, A+=A−1 exactly.

AA+ and A+A are the orthogonal projectors onto col(A) and row(A) — that is the geometry: project onto what A can actually reach, then invert only where inverting means something. The one knob that matters is rcond, the cutoff below which a σi​ is declared zero. Set it too small and a near-null direction gets divided by almost nothing, and your solution explodes.

You reach for it when

  • The system has no solution, or has far too many.
  • The matrix is rank deficient and a plain solve refuses.
  • You want the least-squares answer without writing normal equations.
  • Approximately undoing a projection or a squashing step.

The trap

np.linalg.pinv is not a free pass. It cheerfully returns an answer for a badly conditioned matrix, and that answer is garbage if rcond lets a near-zero singular value through — dividing by 1e-16 blows the solution up. For the plain least-squares case prefer np.linalg.lstsq, which solves without ever materialising the pseudo-inverse.

The math cost: O(mn · min(m,n)) — you are paying for a full SVD

A=UΣV⊤⇒A+=VΣ+U⊤, with Σii+​=1/σi​ when σi​>τ and 0 otherwise.   Tall, full rank: A+=(A⊤A)−1A⊤.   Wide, full rank: A+=A⊤(AA⊤)−1.   Square, invertible: A+=A−1.   Projectors: AA+=Pcol(A)​, A+A=Prow(A)​.

In NumPy / PyTorch

A = np.random.randn(6, 3)   # tall -> overdetermined
b = np.random.randn(6)
x  = np.linalg.pinv(A) @ b                    # least-squares solution
x2, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(A, b, rcond=None)   # same answer, cheaper
np.allclose(x, x2)                            # -> True

W = np.random.randn(3, 6)   # wide -> underdetermined
z = np.linalg.pinv(W) @ b[:3]   # the MINIMUM-NORM exact solution
np.linalg.pinv(A, rcond=1e-10)  # rcond = where you declare a sigma to be zero

Where this lives in real ML code

np.linalg.pinv is what sklearn’s LinearDiscriminantAnalysis and several statsmodels fits fall back to when the design matrix is rank deficient — it is why you get coefficients instead of a LinAlgError after one-hot encoding a column without dropping a level. In deep learning, the closed-form linear probe people fit on frozen activations is a pseudo-inverse, and it explodes precisely when that activation matrix carries near-zero singular values.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

A is 1000 x 5 with full column rank. What does A-plus times b give you, and why?
The least-squares solution. With full column rank A+=(A⊤A)−1A⊤, so A+b minimises ∥Ax−b∥2​. Geometrically, AA+b is the projection of b onto col(A) — the closest point the matrix can actually reach.
Now A is 5 x 1000, so infinitely many exact solutions exist. Which one comes back?
The minimum-norm one. A+b=A⊤(AA⊤)−1b returns the solution with the smallest ∥x∥2​: the one lying entirely in row(A) with no null-space component. Every other solution is that one plus a null-space vector, which only adds length.
Interview trap: is A-plus times A always the identity?
No — only when A has full column rank. In general A+A is the orthogonal projector onto row(A) and AA+ the projector onto col(A); each acts as the identity only on the subspace it projects onto. That asymmetry is exactly why it is called pseudo.

Say this back tomorrow

A+=VΣ+U⊤ — invert the singular values you trust, zero the ones you do not.
  • Overdetermined gives least squares; underdetermined gives minimum norm; invertible gives the plain inverse.
  • AA+ and A+A are projectors, not the identity.
  • rcond decides which σi​ count as zero. One knob, and it decides everything.

  • SVD
  • least squares
  • rank
  • condition number
  • minimum-norm solution
  • regularisation

Eigenvalues & Eigenvectors

Which directions does this matrix leave on their own line?

Push a whole fan of arrows through a matrix and most of them come out pointing somewhere new. A few do not. Those special arrows come out on exactly the same line they started on — only longer, shorter, or flipped end for end. Those arrows are the eigenvectors, and the amount each one got stretched is its eigenvalue. They are the skeleton of what the matrix actually does to space.

Like the axis of a spinning globe. Every city on the surface gets swept somewhere new, but the two points on the axis do not move at all. Find the axis and you have understood the entire spin in one line.

An eigenvector is a v=0 with Av=λv: on that one direction the matrix is pure scaling, no turning. Solve det(A−λI)=0 for the eigenvalues, then read each null space for the vectors. Two facts do most of the interview work. Not every matrix is diagonalisable — a shear [10​11​] has one repeated eigenvalue and only one eigenvector direction. But every real symmetric matrix is: the spectral theorem gives A=QΛQ⊤ with real eigenvalues and orthonormal eigenvectors. That one guarantee is the reason PCA works at all.

Eigenvalues also predict repetition without doing it. Applying A over and over, the largest ∣λ∣ takes over: above one it explodes, below one it collapses, exactly one and it settles — that is power iteration, and it is how PageRank is computed. Two free sanity checks: tr(A)=∑λi​ and det(A)=∏λi​. And a rotation matrix has no real eigenvector at all, because it leaves nothing on its own line; its eigenvalues are complex.

You reach for it when

  • Repeated application. Matrix powers, Markov chains, stability of a dynamical system.
  • Symmetric matrices. Covariance, Gram, kernel and Hessian matrices all live here.
  • Before PCA or spectral clustering. Both are eigenvectors of something, renamed.
  • Graphs. PageRank is the top eigenvector of the link matrix.

The trap

Two classics. Not every matrix is diagonalisable — a shear has one repeated eigenvalue and only one eigenvector direction, so you cannot build a basis out of it. And real matrices can have complex eigenvalues: a 90-degree rotation has no real eigenvector at all, because it leaves nothing on its own line. Interviewers ask for that rotation example by name.

The math square matrices only · O(n³)

Av=λv⟺(A−λI)v=0⟺det(A−λI)=0trace = sum of the eigenvalues · determinant = product of them · symmetric matrix ⇒ real eigenvalues, orthogonal eigenvectors

In NumPy / PyTorch

import numpy as np

A = np.array([[2., 1.], [1., 2.]])      # symmetric
w, V = np.linalg.eigh(A)               # eigh: real w, orthonormal V, sorted ascending
# w = [1., 3.]   V[:, 1] = [0.707, 0.707]

np.allclose(A @ V[:, 1], w[1] * V[:, 1])  # True  ->  Av = lambda v
np.linalg.eig(R)                       # a rotation: returns complex eigenvalues

Where this lives in real ML code

PageRank is one enormous eigenvector problem — the ranking is the dominant eigenvector of the link matrix, found by power iteration because the matrix is far too big to factor. Spectral clustering cuts a graph using the smallest eigenvectors of its Laplacian. And in training, the largest eigenvalue of the Hessian caps your learning rate: on a quadratic, anything above 2/λmax diverges instead of descending.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Explain an eigenvector out loud without using the word “eigenvector”.
It is a direction the matrix refuses to turn. Push it through and it comes back on the same line, only longer, shorter or flipped, and the stretch factor is the eigenvalue. Everything else the matrix does can be described as a mix of what it does to those directions.
Give me a real matrix with no real eigenvectors.
Any 2-D rotation that is not by a multiple of 180 degrees. R=[01​−10​] turns every vector by 90 degrees, so nothing stays on its own line; the eigenvalues are ±i. Real matrix, complex spectrum — which is precisely why we lean on symmetric matrices, where real eigenvalues are guaranteed.
Why do data people care so much that a covariance matrix is symmetric?
Because the spectral theorem then hands you everything at once: real eigenvalues, a full set of orthonormal eigenvectors, and A=QΛQ⊤ with Q−1=Q⊤. That is what makes principal components exist, be mutually perpendicular, and be sortable by variance. Drop symmetry and you lose all three guarantees together.

Say this back tomorrow

Av=λv — the one line A refuses to turn
  • Eigenvector = the direction that survives. Eigenvalue = the stretch on it.
  • They are the roots of det(A−λI)=0; trace is their sum, determinant their product.
  • Symmetric ⇒ real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors. That fact carries PCA.
  • Rotations have no real eigenvector. Shears are not diagonalisable.

  • spectral radius
  • Rayleigh quotient
  • PageRank

Diagonalization

In the right coordinates, a matrix is just stretching.

Most matrices mix your coordinates together, which makes them awkward to work with. Diagonalization finds a better set of directions — the matrix’s own directions — where nothing gets mixed at all. In those directions the matrix only stretches each one by its own amount. So you change into that view, do the easy stretching, and change back. Same answer, no mixing. Repeat the matrix a hundred times and only the stretch amounts change.

Like squeezing a balloon between your palms. Line your hands up with the balloon’s own long axis and the squeeze is simple: shorter one way, fatter the other. Diagonalization is finding that line-up first, doing the plain squeeze, then turning everything back.

A=PΛP−1, where the columns of P are eigenvectors and Λ is diagonal with the eigenvalues. Read it right to left: P−1 rewrites x in the eigenbasis, Λ scales each coordinate on its own, P puts you back in standard coordinates. The pay-off arrives the moment you repeat the map: Ak=PΛkP−1, so a thousand steps costs n scalar powers instead of a thousand matmuls. It exists only when A has n independent eigenvectors. Symmetric matrices always do, and there P is orthogonal, so P−1=P⊤ is free.

Be honest about the failure mode. A defective matrix has no eigenbasis and needs Jordan form in theory; in practice nobody computes Jordan form because it is numerically unstable, and LAPACK gives you the Schur decomposition A=QTQ⊤ instead, which exists for every square matrix. Even when diagonalization does exist, near-parallel eigenvectors make P ill-conditioned and P−1 enormous, so the factorisation is useless in float32 long before it formally stops existing.

You reach for it when

  • Repeated application. Matrix powers, Markov chains, linear recurrences.
  • Reading a transformation. Eigenvalues give the shape, the basis gives the tilt.
  • Symmetric matrices. Whitening, PCA and matrix square roots all run through it.
  • Functions of a matrix. Exponentials and inverses become work on the diagonal.

The trap

Diagonalizable and invertible are unrelated properties, and interviewers probe that. [00​10​] is singular and defective; [10​11​] is perfectly invertible and still not diagonalizable. The practical warning is milder and more common: when two eigenvectors are nearly parallel, P is close to singular and the round trip loses precision long before the theory breaks.

The math needs n independent eigenvectors · O(n³)

A=PΛP−1Ak=PΛkP−1A=QΛQ⊤ when A=A⊤columns of P are eigenvectors · Λ is diagonal · in the symmetric case Q is orthogonal, so the inverse is just the transpose

In NumPy / PyTorch

import numpy as np

w, P = np.linalg.eig(A)
np.allclose(P @ np.diag(w) @ np.linalg.inv(P), A)   # True, if A is diagonalizable

# A to the 50th, without 50 matmuls
A50 = P @ np.diag(w**50) @ np.linalg.inv(P)

# symmetric shortcut: inv(Q) is Q.T, and eigh is the stable routine
w, Q = np.linalg.eigh(Sm)
np.allclose(Q @ np.diag(w) @ Q.T, Sm)               # True
Sm_inv_sqrt = Q @ np.diag(w**-0.5) @ Q.T    # whitening matrix, same machinery

Where this lives in real ML code

Whitening a feature batch is diagonalization with a fractional power: factor the covariance, raise the eigenvalues to the power minus one half, rebuild. ZCA whitening in classic vision pipelines is literally that expression. The failure you actually hit is a near-defective matrix — two eigenvalues nearly collide, the eigenvector basis goes ill-conditioned, and your reconstructed matrix drifts visibly from the original in float32.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

When does diagonalization fail, and what does real numerical code use instead?
It fails when A lacks n independent eigenvectors — a repeated eigenvalue whose eigenspace is too small, like a shear. Jordan normal form is the textbook answer but is numerically unstable and nobody computes it. LAPACK gives you the Schur decomposition A=QTQ⊤ with Q orthogonal and T upper triangular, which exists for every square matrix and still exposes the eigenvalues on the diagonal.
You need A raised to the power 1000. Talk me through it.
Raise the eigenvalues, not the matrix. Ak=PΛkP−1 turns k matrix products into n scalar powers. It also tells you the answer before you compute it: the largest ∣λ∣ dominates, so the result blows up above one, collapses to zero below one, and converges to its eigenvector at exactly one — that last case is a Markov chain reaching steady state.
What is different about diagonalizing a symmetric matrix?
The basis is orthogonal, so the change of basis is free and stable. A=QΛQ⊤ with Q⊤Q=I: no inverse to compute, no conditioning blow-up, real eigenvalues guaranteed, and existence guaranteed even with repeated eigenvalues. The perpendicularity is also what lets PCA claim its components are uncorrelated.

Say this back tomorrow

A=PΛP−1 — change basis, stretch, change back
  • Columns of P are the eigenvectors; Λ holds the eigenvalues.
  • Read right to left: P−1 goes in, Λ scales, P comes back out.
  • The pay-off is powers and functions: Ak=PΛkP−1.
  • Needs n independent eigenvectors. Symmetric matrices always have them, orthogonally.

Singular Value Decomposition

Rotate, stretch, rotate. Every matrix, no exceptions.

Every matrix, whatever shape it is, does the same three things in a row: it turns your data, stretches it along a few clean directions, then turns it again. Singular value decomposition pulls those three steps apart and hands them to you separately. The stretch amounts come out sorted, biggest first, so you can see at a glance which directions the matrix really cares about and which ones it barely touches at all.

Like saving a photo at lower quality. Keep the handful of patterns that carry the picture and throw away the thousands that only add faint texture. It is still obviously the same photo, at a fraction of the size.

A=UΣV⊤ for every real matrix — square or not, full rank or not, invertible or not. V⊤ rotates, Σ scales the axes by the singular values σ1​≥σ2​≥⋯≥0, U rotates again. The σi​ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of A⊤A, and the count of non-zero ones is the rank. Eckart–Young is what makes it the workhorse: truncating to the top k terms gives Ak​, the provably closest rank-k matrix to A in both the Frobenius and spectral norms.

Everything diagnostic falls out of Σ. The condition number is σ1​/σn​; the pseudo-inverse is A+=VΣ+U⊤, which is what a least-squares solver is really doing; the numerical rank is the count of σi​ above a tolerance, not the count of exact zeros. Full SVD costs O(mnmin(m,n)), so for a big sparse matrix you use a truncated or randomised solver that computes only the top k and never forms the dense factors.

You reach for it when

  • The matrix is not square. Eigenvectors do not exist; singular values always do.
  • Compression and denoising. Keep the top directions, drop the tail.
  • Rank, conditioning, pseudo-inverse. All three read straight off the spectrum.
  • A least-squares fit that will not behave. Tiny singular values are the reason.

The trap

The headline trap is confusing it with eigendecomposition — see drill one. Two more: singular values are not the absolute values of eigenvalues in general, only for symmetric matrices. And the sign of a singular vector is arbitrary, so two libraries can hand you U and V columns with flipped signs and both are correct. Never diff SVD output element by element.

The math any m×n · O(mn·min(m,n))

A=UΣV⊤,σ1​≥⋯≥σr​>0,Ak​=∑i=1k​σi​ui​vi⊤​rank = number of non-zero σ · condition number = σmax / σmin · Eckart–Young: nothing of rank k beats the truncation

In NumPy / PyTorch

U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(A, full_matrices=False)
# s is 1-D and already sorted descending;  A == U @ np.diag(s) @ Vt

rank = (s > s[0] * 1e-10).sum()   # numerical rank, not a count of exact zeros
cond = s[0] / s[-1]                # how badly conditioned A is

k  = 40
Ak = U[:, :k] @ np.diag(s[:k]) @ Vt[:k]   # the best rank-40 A there is
kept = (s[:k]**2).sum() / (s**2).sum()  # fraction of the energy retained

Where this lives in real ML code

Truncated SVD is latent semantic analysis, and it is still the fastest sane baseline on a sparse TF-IDF matrix, where centring for PCA would destroy sparsity and blow up memory. It is how recommender matrices get factorised, and it is the justification behind LoRA: weight updates during fine-tuning turn out to be close to low rank, so you store two thin factors instead of a full matrix. It is also the diagnostic when a design matrix is rank-deficient — a near-zero smallest singular value is your warning that the least-squares coefficients are about to explode.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

What is the difference between eigendecomposition and SVD?
Eigendecomposition needs a square matrix and may not exist; SVD works on every matrix and always exists. Eigen gives A=PΛP−1: one basis used on both sides, P not generally orthogonal, eigenvalues possibly negative, complex, or repeated-and-defective. SVD gives A=UΣV⊤: two orthonormal bases — input directions V, output directions U — and singular values that are always real and non-negative. They coincide only for symmetric positive semi-definite A, where U=V=Q and σi​=λi​. In general σi2​ are the eigenvalues of A⊤A.
Why is truncating the SVD the best you can do at that rank?
Eckart–Young. Of all matrices of rank at most k, Ak​=∑i≤k​σi​ui​vi⊤​ minimises ∥A−B∥ in both the Frobenius and spectral norms, and the leftover error is exactly what you discarded: ∥A−Ak​∥2​=σk+1​. No cleverer rank-k matrix exists. That is a theorem, not a heuristic — which is why so much of compression reduces to “take the SVD and stop early”.
Your least-squares coefficients are huge and swing wildly on new data. What does the SVD tell you?
Look at the small singular values. The solution is ∑i​(ui⊤​b/σi​)vi​, so any σi​ near zero divides by almost nothing and amplifies noise along that direction; the condition number σ1​/σn​ is the amplification factor. Fixes: truncate those terms, or add ridge, which replaces 1/σi​ with σi​/(σi2​+λ) and damps them smoothly instead of cutting.

Say this back tomorrow

A=UΣV⊤ — rotate, stretch, rotate. Always.
  • Exists for every matrix: non-square, rank-deficient, singular, anything.
  • σi​ sorted big to small; the count of non-zero ones is the rank.
  • Top-k truncation is the provably best rank-k approximation (Eckart–Young).
  • Symmetric PSD is the one case where SVD and eigendecomposition are the same thing.

  • Eckart–Young
  • low-rank approximation
  • pseudo-inverse
  • condition number
  • truncated SVD
  • latent semantic analysis
  • LoRA

Principal Component Analysis

Which direction does your data actually spread along?

Your data has hundreds of columns but it does not really move in hundreds of directions. Most of it lives in a much thinner shape. Principal component analysis finds the direction the points spread along the most, then the next one at right angles to it, and so on down. Keep the first handful, drop the rest, and you have a small version of the data that still looks like the data. Nothing was measured differently — you only changed the angle you look from.

Like a choir where three voices carry the tune. Forty people are singing, but you could drop most of them and still recognise the song. The catch is that what you kept is a blend, not any one singer.

Centre the data, then take the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix C=n−11​Xc⊤​Xc​ — those are the principal components, and their eigenvalues are the variance along each one. Equivalently, and this is how it is actually computed, take the SVD of the centred matrix Xc​=UΣV⊤: the right singular vectors V are the eigenvectors of C, and σi2​/(n−1) are its eigenvalues. Same answer, better numerics, and you never form X⊤X. Choose k from the explained-variance ratio σi2​/∑j​σj2​.

Because C is symmetric, the spectral theorem guarantees the components are real and mutually orthogonal — that is the whole reason the scores are uncorrelated. The scores are Z=Xc​Vk​=Uk​Σk​; whitening divides each column by its σi​ to give unit variance. Fit on the training split only: computing the components over train and test together leaks test variance into the transform and quietly inflates your score.

You reach for it when

  • Too many correlated columns. Hundreds of features that mostly repeat each other.
  • Visualising high-dimensional data. Squash to two or three axes and plot it.
  • Shrinking embeddings. Smaller vector index, faster search, similar recall.
  • Denoising. The trailing components are frequently just measurement noise.

The trap

Three that catch people. You must centre — skip it and the first component points at the mean instead of at the spread. You usually must standardise when features are on different units, or the column measured in dollars drowns out the one measured in metres. And components are not features: each one is a dense mix of every original column, so “PC1 is customer income” is never true, and PCA is dimensionality reduction, not feature selection.

The math fit on train only · O(nd·min(n,d)) via SVD

C=n−11​Xc⊤​Xc​=VΛV⊤,Xc​=UΣV⊤,λi​=n−1σi2​​the same V both ways · explained variance ratio = one squared singular value divided by the sum of them all · the scores are the centred X times the first k components

In NumPy / PyTorch

from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

Xs = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X_train)  # centres AND scales; fit on train only
p  = PCA(n_components=0.95).fit(Xs)       # keep enough PCs for 95% of the variance
Z  = p.transform(Xs)                          # the scores, shape (n, k)

p.explained_variance_ratio_[:5]           # [0.41, 0.19, 0.08, 0.05, 0.03]
p.components_.shape                           # (k, d) - each row is a direction, not a feature

# by hand, identical result:
Xc = X - X.mean(axis=0)                    # the step everybody forgets
U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(Xc, full_matrices=False)
Z  = Xc @ Vt[:k].T                            # == U[:, :k] * s[:k]

Where this lives in real ML code

The version you meet in 2026 is squeezing a 1536-dimension embedding down to 256 before it goes into a vector index: smaller index, faster search, and recall barely moves, because embeddings really do sit on a much thinner manifold than their nominal width. Eigenfaces were the original poster child. The bug people actually ship is fitting the PCA on the whole dataset before the train/test split — that leaks test variance into the transform and inflates the offline score by a few points that never appear in production.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Someone tells you PCA and SVD are two different algorithms. Correct them.
They are the same computation. PCA on centred X is the SVD of X: the right singular vectors V are the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, and σi2​/(n−1) are its eigenvalues. Every serious library computes PCA through SVD, because forming X⊤X squares the condition number and throws away half your precision for nothing.
How do you choose k, honestly?
Explained-variance ratio first, then judgement. Plot the cumulative σi2​/∑j​σj2​ and take the elbow, or the smallest k that reaches a threshold like 95%. Say out loud that the threshold is a rule of thumb: if PCA feeds a downstream model, the defensible answer is to cross-validate k against that model's metric. What you must not do is pick k by squinting at the components and deciding which ones look meaningful.
When is PCA the wrong tool?
When the direction you need is not the direction with the most variance. PCA is unsupervised, so it will happily discard the low-variance axis that perfectly separates your classes — reach for LDA when labels matter. It also assumes linear structure, so a spiral or a ring defeats it and you want a manifold method instead. And it is the wrong move when the signal is sparse and rare, because rare signal lives in exactly the tail you just threw away.

Say this back tomorrow

Centre first, then take the top singular directions of X
  • Principal components = eigenvectors of the covariance = right singular vectors of centred X.
  • Eigenvalue = variance along that component; its share of the total is the explained-variance ratio.
  • Always centre. Standardise when the units differ. Fit on train only.
  • Components are blends of every column, so they are directions, not interpretable features.

Quadratic Forms & Positive-Definiteness

Is this surface a bowl, a saddle, or a trough?

Feed a matrix a direction and it hands back a single number: how much that direction costs. Sweep every direction and those numbers trace out a surface. If the surface is a bowl, there is exactly one lowest point and rolling downhill always finds it. If it is a saddle, some directions go up and others go down, so there is no bottom to reach. If it is a trough, there is a whole flat line of equally good answers.

Like a marble in a bowl versus a marble on a wobbly table. In the bowl it ends up in the same spot wherever you drop it. On the wobbly table it depends entirely on where you let go, and one nudge sends it off the edge for good.

A quadratic form is q(x)=x⊤Ax with A symmetric — one number out, quadratic in x. Its sign for every non-zero x classifies A: positive definite means q(x)>0 always, which happens exactly when every eigenvalue is positive. Diagonalise and it is obvious — in the eigenbasis q(x)=∑i​λi​yi2​, so each eigenvalue is the curvature along its own axis. All positive gives a bowl with a unique minimum; mixed signs give a saddle; a zero eigenvalue gives a flat direction where the minimum is not unique.

This is why covariance is always PSD: v⊤X⊤Xv=∥Xv∥2≥0, a squared length, which cannot be negative. Kernel and Gram matrices must be PSD for the same reason, and Mercer’s condition is precisely that requirement. Cholesky A=LL⊤ exists if and only if A is positive definite, which is why a failed Cholesky is the standard cheap test. And ridge regularisation A+λI shifts every eigenvalue up by λ, turning a singular matrix into an invertible, strictly positive-definite one.

You reach for it when

  • Second-order optimisation. Reading a Hessian to tell a minimum from a saddle.
  • Covariance and kernels. Both must be positive semi-definite or the maths breaks.
  • Cholesky. Sampling a Gaussian or solving a normal equation needs definiteness.
  • Regularisation. Adding a ridge term is literally lifting every eigenvalue.

The trap

People say “positive definite” when they mean “all the entries are positive”. Completely unrelated: [12​21​] has nothing but positive entries and eigenvalues 3 and −1, so it is indefinite. Also, checking definiteness by computing eigenvalues is the slow way — attempt a Cholesky factorisation and see whether it fails. That is what every library actually does.

The math A symmetric · Cholesky is O(n³/3), half of LU

q(x)=x⊤Ax=∑i​λi​yi2​  in the eigenbasis,A≻0⟺λi​>0 ∀i⟺A=LL⊤all λ > 0 = bowl, one minimum · mixed signs = saddle · one λ = 0 = flat trough, minimum not unique

In NumPy / PyTorch

import numpy as np

def is_pd(A):
    try:
        np.linalg.cholesky(A)      # fails the instant a pivot goes non-positive
        return True
    except np.linalg.LinAlgError:
        return False

C = np.cov(X, rowvar=False)      # PSD by construction, often only *semi*
is_pd(C)                           # False if n < d, or two columns are duplicates
is_pd(C + 1e-6 * np.eye(len(C)))  # True - jitter lifts every eigenvalue by 1e-6

np.linalg.eigvalsh(H).min() > 0    # the slow, explicit test on a Hessian

Where this lives in real ML code

Every Gaussian process and every multivariate-normal sampler calls Cholesky on a covariance matrix, and in float32 a matrix that is positive definite on paper comes back with a tiny negative eigenvalue and raises LinAlgError. The universal fix is jitter, a small multiple of the identity, which is the same arithmetic as ridge regularisation: it shifts every eigenvalue up. In training, the Hessian where a loss curve flattens is almost never positive definite — large models stall on saddles, not minima, which is exactly why naive second-order methods do not just work and why gradient noise helps.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Prove that any covariance matrix is positive semi-definite.
Because it is a Gram matrix. With centred data C=n−11​X⊤X, so for any v, v⊤Cv=n−11​∥Xv∥2≥0. It is a squared length, so it cannot be negative. It is only semi-definite because equality is reachable: if one feature is a copy of another, or you have fewer rows than columns, some Xv is exactly zero and that direction has eigenvalue 0.
Your Hessian is positive definite at a critical point. What does that mean — and what if one eigenvalue is negative?
Positive definite means a strict local minimum: every direction curves upward, so it is a bowl and any small step costs you. One negative eigenvalue makes it a saddle, and the escape route is the eigenvector belonging to that negative eigenvalue. In deep networks almost all critical points are saddles rather than maxima, which is why stochastic gradient noise is useful — it knocks you off the ridge instead of leaving you parked on it.
Cholesky fails on a matrix you know is a covariance. Why, and what do you do?
Floating point. The true matrix is positive semi-definite, rounding pushes a near-zero eigenvalue slightly negative, and Cholesky needs strictly positive pivots. Add jitter: A+ϵI lifts every eigenvalue by ϵ, the smallest honest fix. Alternatives are an eigendecomposition with the negatives clipped to zero, or a pivoted LDL factorisation. Be explicit that jitter is a numerical patch, not a modelling decision.

Say this back tomorrow

x⊤Ax>0 for every x=0 — a bowl, one bottom
  • Positive definite ⇔ every eigenvalue positive ⇔ Cholesky succeeds.
  • Positive semi-definite allows λ=0: a flat direction, minimum not unique.
  • Mixed signs = saddle. That is what a stalled training run is usually sitting on.
  • Covariance and kernel matrices are PSD by construction; ridge or jitter makes them PD.

  • Cholesky
  • covariance matrix
  • kernel / Gram matrix
  • convexity
  • ridge & jitter
  • Rayleigh quotient
  • saddle points

LU, QR & Cholesky

Nobody inverts a matrix. They factor it first.

Solving a big pile of equations directly is slow, and it goes wrong when the numbers are awkward. So nobody does it that way twice. You take the matrix apart once into two simpler pieces, each one easy to run through, and then every question you ask afterwards is cheap. The expensive work happens once, up front. Which pair of pieces you pick depends on what you plan to ask.

Like stripping an engine down onto the bench. Once it is in labelled parts, swapping a component or answering “why does it knock?” takes minutes. Left as one sealed lump, every question means starting from scratch.

Three factorisations carry almost all of numerical linear algebra. PA=LU is Gaussian elimination cached — O(n3) once, then every new right-hand side is two triangular sweeps at O(n2). A=QR with Q⊤Q=I and R upper-triangular is the stable road to least squares: it works on X directly and never forms X⊤X, so it never squares the condition number. A=LL⊤ (Cholesky) demands a symmetric positive-definite A and pays you back with half the flops of LU.

The practical consequence: solve, never invert. np.linalg.solve is an LU with partial pivoting; lstsq is a QR or SVD; cho_factor is Cholesky. Factorisations also hand you things an inverse does not: detA=∏i​Uii​ falls out of LU, and logdetA=2∑i​logLii​ falls out of Cholesky without ever overflowing. Cholesky doubles as a test — if it fails, your matrix was not positive-definite, which is usually the bug you actually wanted to hear about.

You reach for it when

  • The same matrix keeps coming back and only the right-hand side changes
  • You want a least-squares fit without squaring the error amplification
  • You have a covariance matrix and need to sample from it or score a likelihood
  • You need a determinant or a log-determinant that will not overflow

The trap

Never write inv(A) @ b. solve(A, b) is faster and more accurate, because forming the inverse does the same work and then throws extra rounding on top. And Cholesky is not general: hand it a matrix that is symmetric but not positive-definite and you get LinAlgError: Matrix is not positive definite — almost always a covariance that lost rank or drifted off symmetry through accumulated rounding.

The math Cholesky ~n³/3 · LU ~2n³/3 · QR ~4n³/3

PA=LU  ·  A=QR,Q⊤Q=I  ·  A=LL⊤
Ax=b⇒Ly=Pb, then Ux=y — two O(n2) sweeps
logdetA=2∑i​logLii​factor once at n^3, then pay n^2 per solve, forever

In NumPy / PyTorch

# factor once, reuse for every right-hand side
import numpy as np, scipy.linalg as sla

lu, piv = sla.lu_factor(A)                # O(n^3), paid once
X = np.stack([sla.lu_solve((lu, piv), b)  # O(n^2) per solve
              for b in B])

Q, R = np.linalg.qr(Xd)                   # least squares, stable
beta = sla.solve_triangular(R, Q.T @ y)

L = np.linalg.cholesky(Sigma)             # SPD only
sample = mu + L @ np.random.randn(n)      # correlated draw
logdet = 2 * np.log(np.diag(L)).sum()    # det() would underflow

Where this lives in real ML code

Every np.linalg.solve is an LU with partial pivoting underneath, and every lstsq is a QR or an SVD. Cholesky is the one you meet most in ML: torch.distributions.MultivariateNormal factors the covariance both to draw samples and to compute log_prob, and an exact Gaussian process marginal likelihood is a Cholesky of the kernel matrix. That is exactly why exact GPs fall over past roughly ten thousand points, and why you see “adding jitter to the diagonal” in GPyTorch logs — that jitter is someone nudging a barely-positive-definite matrix back over the line.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

You have to solve Ax = b for 500 different b, with A fixed. What do you do, and what does it save?
Answer. Factor once, then reuse. PA=LU costs ≈32​n3; after that each solve is a forward and a back substitution at O(n2). For n=1000 that is one 109-ish job plus 500 cheap ones, instead of 500 full eliminations. In SciPy: lu_factor once, lu_solve in the loop.
Interview trap: why do people say QR beats the normal equations for least squares?
Answer. The normal equations solve X⊤Xβ=X⊤y, and κ(X⊤X)=κ(X)2 — you square the error amplification before you start, costing you half your significant digits. QR works on X itself, so the conditioning you live with is κ(X). On a well-conditioned X nobody notices; on collinear features it is the difference between a fit and garbage.
When can you use Cholesky, and what do you get for the restriction?
Answer. Only for symmetric positive-definite A — covariances, Gram matrices X⊤X, Hessians at a minimum. You get roughly n3/3 flops (half of LU), no pivoting needed, better stability, and a free cheap logdet. Bonus: a failed Cholesky is a reliable signal that your “covariance” is not one.

Say this back tomorrow

PA=LU · A=QR · A=LL⊤ — factor once, then solve forever.
  • LU for repeated solves: O(n3) once, O(n2) per right-hand side.
  • QR for least squares: never forms X⊤X, so never squares κ.
  • Cholesky for symmetric positive-definite: half the flops, and it fails loudly when the matrix is not SPD.

Matrix Calculus: Gradients, Jacobians & Hessians

Backprop is the chain rule wearing a matrix.

A derivative tells you which way a number moves when you nudge one input. Do that for every input at once and you get a list of slopes, one per input. That list is the gradient. Now let the thing you are measuring have many outputs instead of one, and the list becomes a table: a row of slopes per output. Take slopes of the slopes and you get curvature. Training a model is reading those slopes and stepping the other way.

Like a hiker in thick fog feeling for the way down. Shift a boot in each direction and note which way the ground drops. The gradient is all of those readings at once, and you walk against it.

Shapes first, because shapes are the whole game. For f:Rn→R the gradient ∇f is n×1. For f:Rn→Rm the Jacobian J is m×n with Jij​=∂fi​/∂xj​ — row i is just the gradient of output i. The Hessian H=∇2f is n×n and symmetric. Three results worth having by heart: ∂x∂​(Ax)=A, ∂x∂​(x⊤Ax)=(A+A⊤)x, and ∂x∂​∥x∥2=2x. The chain rule is then Jacobian multiplication: Jf∘g​=Jf​Jg​.

None of those Jacobians ever get built. With one scalar loss and n≈109 parameters, reverse mode seeds v=1 at the loss and pushes vector-Jacobian products v⊤J backwards, so a whole backward pass costs about what a forward pass costs, whatever n is; forward mode would need one pass per input. The Hessian stays implicit for the same reason — n2 entries is not a thing you can store — so second-order methods use Hessian-vector products Hv (one extra autodiff pass over ∇f), L-BFGS keeps a low-rank history of past gradients instead, and Adam settles for a diagonal estimate.

You reach for it when

  • You are checking a hand-derived gradient against what autograd returns
  • You need to explain why a backward pass costs what it costs
  • Someone proposes a second-order optimizer and you have to price it
  • A loss goes to NaN and you want to know which term blew up

The trap

Two classics. Layout: is ∂y/∂x shaped m×n or its transpose? Pick numerator layout, stay in it, and most hand-derived gradient bugs turn out to be one missing transpose. Direction: the gradient points uphill, which is why gradient descent subtracts it — and it only exists for scalar outputs, so backward() on a non-scalar tensor raises grad can be implicitly created only for scalar outputs.

The math gradient n×1 · Jacobian m×n · Hessian n×n

∇f=[∂x1​∂f​,…,∂xn​∂f​]⊤  ·  Jij​=∂xj​∂fi​​  ·  Hij​=∂xi​∂xj​∂2f​
∂x∂​(Ax)=A  ·  ∂x∂​(x⊤Ax)=(A+A⊤)x  ·  ∂x∂​∥x∥2=2x
Jf∘g​=Jf​Jg​  ·  reverse mode computes v⊤Jone scalar loss, n parameters: reverse mode costs 1 pass, forward mode costs n

In NumPy / PyTorch

import torch
A = torch.randn(4, 4)
x = torch.randn(4, requires_grad=True)
y = x @ A @ x                       # scalar out
y.backward()
torch.allclose(x.grad, (A + A.T) @ x.detach())   # True. not 2Ax

from torch.func import jacrev, jacfwd, vjp, hvp
jacrev(f)(x)      # reverse: cheap when outputs are few
jacfwd(f)(x)      # forward: cheap when inputs are few
_, vjp_fn = vjp(f, x); vjp_fn(v)    # v^T J. the full J is never built
hvp(loss, (x,), (v,))               # H @ v without ever forming H

Where this lives in real ML code

Every loss.backward() is a reverse-mode sweep chaining vector-Jacobian products layer by layer; torch.func.jacrev versus jacfwd is literally that choice exposed as an API. Where it bites: fine-tuning a 7B model, it is the optimizer state and not the weights that runs you out of VRAM — Adam holds two extra float32 numbers per parameter for its diagonal moment estimates, about 56 GB on top of the model. A full Hessian for that same model would have 4.9e19 entries, which is why “just use Newton’s method” is not a real suggestion.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Interview trap: what is the derivative of x-transpose A x with respect to x?
Answer. (A+A⊤)x. It collapses to 2Ax only when A is symmetric — which it often is in practice (covariances, Gram matrices), which is exactly why people memorise the wrong version and get caught the one time it is not.
f maps R^n to R^m. What shape is the Jacobian, what is one row of it, and what does reverse mode actually compute?
Answer. J is m×n; row i is ∇fi⊤​, the gradient of output i. Reverse mode never builds J — it computes the vector-Jacobian product v⊤J, one row-shaped object, for the v handed back from downstream.
Say it out loud: why is reverse-mode autodiff the right default for deep learning, and when would forward mode win?
Answer. Cost scales with the number of outputs in reverse mode and the number of inputs in forward mode. Training has one scalar loss and millions of inputs, so one backward sweep gets every partial derivative — forward mode would need a pass per parameter. Flip the shape (n small, m large — sensitivity analysis, a Jacobian of a tiny input vector) and jacfwd wins.

Say this back tomorrow

∇f: n×1 · J: m×n · H: n×n — and backprop only ever forms v⊤J.
  • One number in the gradient per input; one row in the Jacobian per output.
  • ∂(Ax)/∂x=A, ∂(x⊤Ax)/∂x=(A+A⊤)x, ∂∥x∥2/∂x=2x.
  • One scalar loss and many parameters means reverse mode. H is n2, so nobody builds it — hence Hv, L-BFGS, and Adam’s diagonal.

  • Reverse-mode autodiff
  • Vector-Jacobian product
  • Hessian-vector product
  • L-BFGS
  • Adam
  • Newton step
