Condition Number & Numerical Stability

How much does a tiny input error blow up?

Every number in a computer is a little bit wrong, because it got rounded to fit. The condition number tells you how much that little wrongness grows when your matrix touches it. A small number means the answer coming out is about as trustworthy as the data going in. A huge number means the rounding noise comes out louder than the answer, and everything downstream is fiction, even though the code ran without complaining.

Like a wobbly kitchen scale. A gram off on the flour and the bread is fine; a gram off on the yeast and you get a brick. The condition number is how much that same gram matters.

κ(A)=σmax​/σmin​, the ratio of the largest to the smallest singular value, and it is an error amplifier: ∥x∥∥δx∥​≤κ(A)∥b∥∥δb∥​. Orthogonal matrices have κ=1 — a rotation preserves length, so error in equals error out. Singular matrices have κ=∞. The working rule: you lose about log10​κ decimal digits. float64 gives you roughly 16 digits and float32 roughly 7, so κ=108 in float32 means every digit you get back is noise.

Two consequences you will actually use. First, never form X⊤X: κ(X⊤X)=κ(X)2, so the normal equations spend half your digits before the solve starts — QR or SVD work on X directly and keep κ(X). Second, ridge fixes conditioning, not just overfitting: adding λI lifts the smallest singular value, giving κ(X⊤X+λI)=σmin2​+λσmax2​+λ​, which is why a tiny λ can turn a solve that returns nonsense into one that returns an answer.

You reach for it when

  • A linear model gives wild coefficients on features that are near-duplicates
  • You are moving a model to half precision and need to know what breaks first
  • A solver returns a different answer when you reorder the rows
  • Gradients explode, or the loss turns to NaN and the data looks clean

The trap

A small determinant does not mean ill-conditioned, and a big one does not mean healthy. Scale a perfectly well-conditioned 1000×1000 matrix by 0.1 and its determinant drops by 10−1000 while κ does not budge. Judge conditioning with np.linalg.cond, never with det.

The math κ = σmax / σmin · digits lost ≈ log10 κ

κ(A)=σmin​σmax​​  ·  ∥x∥∥δx∥​≤κ(A)∥b∥∥δb∥​
κ(Q)=1  ·  κ(X⊤X)=κ(X)2  ·  κ(X⊤X+λI)=σmin2​+λσmax2​+λ​float64 ~ 16 digits, float32 ~ 7, bfloat16 ~ 3

In NumPy / PyTorch

# two near-identical features: the classic bad design matrix
X = np.c_[x1, x1 + 1e-6 * np.random.randn(n)]
np.linalg.cond(X)              # ~1e6
np.linalg.cond(X.T @ X)        # ~1e12, squared

# stable: QR/SVD under the hood, keeps cond(X)
beta = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)[0]

# ridge: lifts the smallest singular value, conditioning improves
beta = np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X + 1e-3 * np.eye(2), X.T @ y)

np.linalg.svd(X, compute_uv=False)   # look at sigma_min before you blame the model

Where this lives in real ML code

The everyday face of this is LinAlgError: Singular matrix from np.linalg.inv on a design matrix carrying a duplicated one-hot column, or scikit-learn warning that a least-squares solve is ill-conditioned. In deep nets it shows up as exploding gradients: repeated multiplication by badly conditioned Jacobians, which is precisely what gradient clipping, orthogonal init and LayerNorm exist to contain. And the reason every softmax implementation subtracts the row max before exponentiating is the same family of problem — without it, exp overflows to inf in float16 and your loss is NaN by step 400.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

What is the condition number of an orthogonal matrix, and why does that matter to a deep net?
Answer. κ(Q)=1: all singular values are 1, so a rotation or reflection neither amplifies nor damps error, and the norm of whatever passes through is preserved. That is the whole argument for orthogonal initialisation and for rotation-based tricks like RoPE — stack a hundred of them and nothing explodes or vanishes.
Interview trap: your float32 pipeline has a matrix with condition number 1e8. What have you got left?
Answer. Nothing. float32 carries about 7 decimal digits; log10​108=8 digits lost, so the result is pure rounding noise even though no exception is raised. Options: move that step to float64, regularise to lift σmin​, drop or merge the collinear columns, or switch to a decomposition that does not square κ.
Say it out loud: training loss goes NaN at step 400. Walk me through the checks.
Answer. Check the gradient norm just before the blow-up (clip it and see if it survives); check for a division or a log of something near zero; check precision — float16 overflows around 65504, bfloat16 has the range but only ~3 digits; check the data for an unscaled or duplicated feature that has made the input to the layer badly conditioned. NaN is almost always overflow, a zero denominator, or an amplifier you did not know was there.

Say this back tomorrow

κ=σmax​/σmin​ — you lose log10​κ digits, and float32 only ever had 7.
  • Orthogonal: κ=1, error in equals error out. Singular: κ=∞.
  • κ(X⊤X)=κ(X)2 — the normal equations spend half your digits before they begin. Use QR.
  • Ridge lifts σmin​, which is why a tiny λ can rescue a hopeless solve.

Unlocks

  • Singular values
  • Normal equations
  • Ridge regression
  • Gradient clipping
  • float32 vs bfloat16
  • Pseudo-inverse

Complexity & FLOPs

Know the price before you start the job.

Every operation has a price, and the price depends on how big the thing you hand it is. Adding two lists costs roughly what you would guess. Multiplying two square tables costs the size cubed, so doubling the table makes it eight times slower, not twice. Attention costs the square of the sentence length, which is why long context gets expensive fast. Knowing which curve you are on is the difference between a job that takes a minute and one that takes a week.

Like a shipping bill priced by volume, not weight. Double every side of the box and you do not pay twice as much, you pay eight times as much. That is what cubic cost feels like the first time you double a matrix.

A matmul (m,n)@(n,p) costs about 2mnp FLOPs — one multiply and one add per term. Everything square and clever is cubic: inverse, LU, QR, eigendecomposition and SVD are all Θ(n3), differing only in the constant (Cholesky ≈n3/3, LU ≈32​n3, QR ≈34​n3, SVD an order more). Attention is O(s2d) per layer in time and, done naively, in memory too — double the context and the score matrix quadruples, which is the entire reason FlashAttention and the KV cache exist.

Two numbers worth carrying into an interview, both rules of thumb rather than theorems. A forward-plus-backward pass costs roughly 3× a forward pass, because the backward needs both an input gradient and a weight gradient (about two matmuls for every forward matmul). And training a dense transformer costs about 6ND FLOPs for N parameters and D tokens: 2ND forward, 4ND backward. Both ignore attention’s s2 term, normalisations, softmaxes and every efficiency loss on real hardware, so use them as an order-of-magnitude sanity check, never as a quote.

You reach for it when

  • Pricing a training run before you go and ask for the GPUs
  • Choosing between a bigger batch and a longer context window
  • Someone wants a matrix inverse inside the training loop
  • The GPU reads as busy but throughput is nowhere near the spec sheet

The trap

FLOPs are not time. A modern GPU does tens of TFLOP/s but only reads a few TB/s from HBM, so anything with low arithmetic intensity — elementwise ops, normalisations, and single-token decoding, where every weight is read once to produce one token — is memory-bandwidth-bound and will not get faster if you shave FLOPs off it. The Θ(n3) matmul is the efficient part of your model: it reuses every byte it loads n times.

The math matmul 2mnp · decompositions Θ(n³) · attention O(s²d)

(m,n)@(n,p)≈2mnp  ·  attention ≈4s2d per layer
forward + backward ≈3× forward  ·  training ≈6ND  (N params, D tokens)
arithmetic intensity =bytes movedFLOPs​6ND and the 3x rule are rules of thumb, not theorems: they ignore attention, norms and MFU

In NumPy / PyTorch

# one matmul, then a whole training run
m, n, p = 1024, 4096, 4096
flops   = 2 * m * n * p        # 3.4e10 for one matmul
fwd_bwd = 3 * flops            # rule of thumb, not a theorem

N, D  = 7e9, 2e12          # params, training tokens
train = 6 * N * D              # 8.4e22 FLOPs
days  = train / (1024 * 1e15 * 0.4) / 86400   # ~2.4 days on 1024 GPUs at 40% MFU

# and the number that actually caps decoding:
bytes_per_token = 7e9 * 2  # bf16 weights, all read once
tok_per_s = 3.3e12 / bytes_per_token   # HBM bandwidth, not FLOPs

Where this lives in real ML code

Compute budgets get quoted with exactly this arithmetic: 70B parameters over 1.4T tokens is 6ND≈5.9×1023 FLOPs, which is how a run becomes “GPU-months” on a slide before anyone touches a keyboard. Inference flips the bottleneck: single-token decoding reads roughly one byte of weights per FLOP, so a 70B model in bf16 has to move about 140 GB per token, and at ~3 TB/s of HBM that caps you near 20 tokens per second no matter how idle the tensor cores are. That is why vLLM batches aggressively, and why the thing you actually run out of is KV cache, not FLOPs.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Roughly how many FLOPs is a (1024, 4096) @ (4096, 4096) matmul, and how do you get there in your head?
Answer. 2mnp=2×1024×4096×4096≈3.4×1010, about 34 GFLOP. The habit worth building: multiply the three dimensions, double it. On a 1 PFLOP/s card at 40% utilisation that is well under a millisecond — which tells you the matmul is not your problem.
Interview trap: you double the context window from 4k to 8k. What happens to attention cost, and what happens to the KV cache?
Answer. They are different curves. Attention is O(s2d), so the score computation goes up 4×. The KV cache is O(s) per layer — it only doubles. People reflexively say “everything quadruples”; the memory that actually evicts your other requests grows linearly.
Say it out loud: why is training compute-bound while single-stream inference is not?
Answer. Arithmetic intensity. Training pushes big batches through, so every weight loaded from HBM gets reused across many tokens and the tensor cores stay fed. Decoding one token at a time reuses each weight exactly once, so you are paying bandwidth for the whole model per token and the FLOPs are nearly free. Hence batching, speculative decoding, and quantisation — all of which cut bytes moved, not FLOPs.

Say this back tomorrow

matmul =2mnp · anything square and clever is Θ(n3) · attention O(s2d) · training ≈6ND.
  • Forward + backward ≈3× forward. A rule of thumb, and say so out loud.
  • Double the context: attention work ×4, KV cache only ×2.
  • At inference you are usually bandwidth-bound, so shaving FLOPs buys you nothing.

Tensor Shapes & Broadcasting

Why one stray shape becomes a whole matrix.

NumPy and PyTorch let you combine arrays of different sizes. They line the two shapes up from the right and check them pair by pair. Sizes that match are fine. A size of one gets reused to match the other side. Missing slots on the left are filled in. That is the whole rule. It is enormously convenient, and it is also why a wrong shape often does not crash. It just quietly builds something much bigger and keeps going.

Like dragging one cell down a spreadsheet column. You typed the tax rate once and the sheet reuses that single value in all ten thousand rows. Broadcasting is the same reuse, except nobody shows you the little fill handle.

Shapes are compared right-to-left. Two axes are compatible if they are equal or one of them is 1; a missing leading axis is treated as 1. The size-1 axis is strided over with stride 0, not copied, so it costs nothing until the result forces a materialisation. In a transformer, activations are (B,H,S,D) and an additive causal mask is (1,1,S,S): batch and head broadcast, so one mask buffer serves every sequence and every head. The failure mode is the mirror image — (n,1) against (1,n) is perfectly legal and hands you (n,n).

That (n,n) is where jobs die. Subtracting a column of 50,000 embeddings from a row of the same asks for 2.5×109 float32 entries — 10 GB — from a line that reads like a subtraction of two vectors. Defend with keepdims discipline, explicit reshape or None indexing, and an assert on the output shape rather than the inputs. torch.broadcast_shapes and np.broadcast_shapes tell you the answer before you allocate it.

You reach for it when

  • You add a bias vector across a whole batch of activations
  • You apply one causal or padding mask over every head
  • You normalise by a per-row mean and forgot keepdims
  • A tensor op returns a shape you did not expect and memory spikes

The trap

x - x.mean(axis=1) on an (n, d) array: the mean is (n,), which right-aligns against d, so you either crash or — far worse — subtract along the wrong axis and get a plausible wrong answer. Use keepdims=True. And the interviewer favourite: (n,1) - (1,n) is not an error, it is an outer difference.

The math no copy — stride 0 on the stretched axis

scores(8,12,512,512)​​+mask(1,1,512,512)​​=(8,12,512,512)right-align, then every pair must be equal or contain a 1

In NumPy / PyTorch

# the mask that works
scores = torch.randn(8, 12, 512, 512)      # B, H, S, S
mask   = torch.full((1, 1, 512, 512), -1e9).triu(1)
scores = scores + mask                   # broadcasts, allocates nothing extra

# the bug that does not crash
col = torch.randn(50_000, 1)
row = torch.randn(1, 50_000)
torch.broadcast_shapes(col.shape, row.shape)   # (50000, 50000) -- check BEFORE you run it
d = col - row                            # 2.5e9 floats = 10 GB, no error

Where this lives in real ML code

Every attention implementation ships a mask shaped (1, 1, S, S) so one buffer covers the whole batch and all heads. And the classic OOM in a retrieval pipeline is a pairwise-distance line: emb[:, None] - emb[None, :] over 50k vectors asks for a 50k-by-50k-by-d tensor. torch.cdist and chunked matmuls exist precisely so you never write that line.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Are shapes (8, 1, 6) and (7, 1) compatible? What comes out?
Yes — the result is (8, 7, 6). Right-align: 6 vs 1 → 6; 1 vs 7 → 7; 8 vs nothing → 8. Every pair is equal or contains a 1, so it passes. Note that both operands stretched — broadcasting is not one-directional.
Your loss stopped moving and memory doubled right after you added per-row normalisation. Where do you look first?
At the shape of the reduction. x - x.mean(1) drops an axis, so the (n,) mean right-aligns against the feature axis instead of the row axis. You get a legal tensor computed along the wrong dimension. Fix with x.mean(1, keepdims=True) and assert out.shape == x.shape.
Explain to an interviewer why broadcasting a mask costs no memory, but the outer-difference bug costs 10 GB.
Because the stretch is stride 0, but the output is real. The stretched axis is a view that re-reads the same element, so the mask itself is never copied. Memory is only spent when the result shape is genuinely bigger — and (n,1)−(1,n) has a result of (n,n), which has to be materialised. Same rule, opposite bill.

Say this back tomorrow

align right → equal, or a 1, or it fails
  • A 1 stretches. A missing leading axis is a 1.
  • Stretching is free (stride 0); a bigger output is not.
  • (n,1) vs (1,n) gives (n,n) — legal, and almost never what you meant.

  • keepdims
  • einsum
  • causal mask
  • broadcast_shapes
  • outer product
  • (B, H, S, D)

Attention as Matrix Math

Two matrix multiplies and one softmax. That is all.

Every token makes three things: a question, a label, and some content. Compare one token's question against every token's label and you get a grid of raw scores, one per pair. Squash each row so those scores turn into weights that add up to one. Then take a weighted blend of everyone's content. That blend is the token's new representation. The whole layer is two multiplications and one squashing step in the middle.

Like a room where everyone shouts a topic and you decide who to listen to. You weigh each voice by how well their topic matches what you are looking for, then take the weighted mixture of what those people actually said.

Attention is softmax(dk​​QK⊤​)V. With X of shape (S,d), three projections give Q,K∈RS×dk​ and V∈RS×dv​. Then QK⊤ is (S,S) — one dot product per token pair, which is exactly why time and score memory are O(S2). Softmax runs along the last axis, so each row is a distribution over keys. Multiplying by V collapses back to (S,dv​): every output row is a convex combination of value rows.

The dk​​ is variance control, not superstition. If q and k have i.i.d. unit-variance entries, q⋅k sums dk​ independent products, so its variance is dk​ and its spread grows like dk​​ — at dk​=128 that is roughly 11× wider than unit scale. Softmax on wide logits saturates toward one-hot and its Jacobian collapses, so gradients vanish. Multi-head is a reshape, not a new idea: split d into h heads of dk​=d/h to get (B,h,S,dk​), run the identical math in parallel across the head axis, concatenate, then apply WO​.

You reach for it when

  • You are asked to write attention from scratch on a whiteboard
  • You need to explain why long context costs so much
  • You are debugging a shape error in a custom head
  • You are choosing between FlashAttention and a naive kernel

The trap

Two of them. First, softmax runs over the key axis (the last one) — softmax over queries produces a perfectly shaped tensor and a broken model, and nothing crashes. Second, people say “attention is O(S2), so FlashAttention makes it linear”. It does not. FlashAttention removes the S×S materialisation in HBM; the FLOPs are still quadratic.

The math O(S2d) time · O(S2) score memory per head

Attn(Q,K,V)=softmax(dk​​QK⊤​)V(S, dₖ) × (dₖ, S) → (S, S) → × (S, dᵥ) → (S, dᵥ)

In NumPy / PyTorch

def attention(q, k, v, mask=None):
    # q, k, v: (B, H, S, D)
    d_k = q.shape[-1]
    s = q @ k.transpose(-2, -1) / math.sqrt(d_k)   # (B, H, S, S)  <-- the quadratic one
    if mask is not None:
        s = s + mask                             # (1, 1, S, S) broadcasts
    w = s.softmax(dim=-1)                      # over KEYS. dim=-2 is the classic bug
    return w @ v                                # (B, H, S, D)

Where this lives in real ML code

At S=4096 with 32 heads, the score tensor alone is 32×16.8M×2 bytes ≈ 1 GB per layer, per sequence. That single number is why FlashAttention exists: it tiles the computation and never writes the S×S block to HBM. It is also why prefill is compute-bound while decode is not, and why every long-context pricing page charges you superlinearly.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Why divide by dk​​ and not by dk​?
Because softmax cares about the standard deviation, not the variance. With unit-variance entries, q⋅k sums dk​ independent products, so Var=dk​ and the spread is dk​​. Dividing by dk​​ restores roughly unit scale. Dividing by dk​ would over-shrink the logits and flatten attention toward uniform.
B=4, h=8, S=1024, d=512. What is the shape after QK⊤, and how many bytes in fp16?
(4,8,1024,1024) — 33.5M entries, 67 MB. dk​=512/8=64 is summed away in the product; only S survives on both axes. Multiplying by V returns (4,8,1024,64), which concatenates back to (4,1024,512) before WO​.
Explain out loud why multi-head attention is not eight separate models.
Because it is one reshape and one batched matmul. (B,S,d) becomes (B,h,S,d/h) and the same math runs across the head axis — there are no extra parameters beyond the single WQ​,WK​,WV​,WO​ you already had. Heads buy you several low-dimensional subspaces to compare in, and WO​ mixes them back together.

Say this back tomorrow

softmax(QKᵀ / √dₖ) V — compare, normalise, blend
  • The (S,S) block is the entire cost story.
  • Scale by dk​​ or softmax saturates and gradients die.
  • Softmax along the key axis. Multi-head is a reshape, not a committee.

KV Cache Memory Math

Pay once per token, or pay again at every step.

When a model writes text it makes one token at a time, and each new token has to look back at every token before it. The keys and values for those earlier tokens never change, so the model stores them and reuses them. Without the store, writing a thousand tokens means redoing the same work a thousand times. With it, each step adds one new column. The catch is that the store grows with every token, and it gets big fast.

Like keeping the receipt instead of re-walking the aisles. You already found and priced everything in the trolley; the only new thing this trip is the one item you just picked up. Throw the receipt away and you shop the whole store again for every item.

During autoregressive decoding, K and V for positions 1…t−1 are unchanged by the new token, so they are cached and only the length-1 slice for t is computed. Cache size is 2⋅L⋅Hkv​⋅dh​⋅S⋅B⋅b bytes, where the 2 is K and V. For a 7B-class model (L=32, Hkv​=32, dh​=128, fp16) that is 2⋅32⋅32⋅128⋅2=512 KB per token: 2 GB at 4k context, and 64 GB at batch 32 — on a card whose weights only took 14 GB.

MQA shares a single K,V head across all query heads; GQA shares one per group, so the cache shrinks by exactly H/Hkv​. Llama-3-8B runs H=32,Hkv​=8: 128 KB per token, a 4× cut, at almost no quality cost. This matters because decode is memory-bandwidth-bound, not compute-bound: every step must read all the weights plus the whole cache to emit one token, so arithmetic intensity sits near 1 FLOP per byte and the GPU idles waiting on loads. Bigger batches are therefore nearly free in latency — until the cache stops fitting.

You reach for it when

  • You are sizing GPU memory for an inference deployment
  • Throughput collapses as users ask for longer contexts
  • You are choosing between MHA, GQA and MQA for a new model
  • You need to say why decoding is slow despite doing few FLOPs

The trap

People size the box for the weights and forget the cache. A 7B model in fp16 is 14 GB of weights, but 32 concurrent users at 4k context add another 64 GB — the cache, not the model, is what OOMs you. Second trap: the cache scales with Hkv​, not H, so quoting the query-head count for a GQA model overstates it by 4–8×.

The math linear in S and B · re-read at every single step

bytes=2⋅L⋅Hkv​⋅dh​⋅S⋅B⋅b7B fp16: 2 · 32 · 32 · 128 · 2 = 512 KB / token → 2 GB @ 4k → 64 GB @ batch 32

In NumPy / PyTorch

# the whole card, as one function
def kv_bytes(layers, kv_heads, head_dim, seq, batch, dtype_bytes=2):
    return 2 * layers * kv_heads * head_dim * seq * batch * dtype_bytes

kv_bytes(32, 32, 128, 4096, 1) / 1e9   # 2.15 GB   MHA   (Llama-2-7B)
kv_bytes(32, 8,  128, 4096, 1) / 1e9   # 0.54 GB   GQA-8 (Llama-3-8B)  4x less
kv_bytes(32, 1,  128, 4096, 1) / 1e9   # 0.07 GB   MQA               32x less

Where this lives in real ML code

vLLM's PagedAttention exists because of this one line. Allocating a contiguous cache per request wastes most of the space to internal fragmentation and over-reservation; paging it into fixed blocks lifted serving throughput several-fold on the same card. Every “context window doubled” announcement is, underneath, a KV-cache engineering story: GQA, paging, quantised KV, or sliding-window attention.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Batch 8, 8k context, Llama-3-8B-shaped (L=32, Hkv​=8, dh​=128, fp16). Cache size?
About 8.6 GB. Per token: 2⋅32⋅8⋅128⋅2=131,072 bytes = 128 KB. Times 8192 tokens = 1.07 GB per sequence. Times batch 8 = 8.6 GB. The weights are 16 GB, so the cache is already more than half the model — and it is the part that grows.
Decoding is memory-bandwidth-bound. What does that imply about batch size?
Raise it. Each step reads all the weights and the whole cache no matter how many sequences you are decoding, so the arithmetic per byte moved is tiny. Adding sequences reuses those same reads and buys throughput at almost no extra latency — until the cache itself no longer fits, which is the real ceiling on batch size.
An interviewer asks: why not cache Q as well?
Because nothing would ever read it again. At each step there is exactly one new query, it produces one output row, and it is done. K and V get re-read by every future token; Q never is. Caching it would store a value with no second reader — pure cost.

Say this back tomorrow

2 × layers × kv_heads × head_dim × seq × batch × bytes
  • The 2 is K and V. Nothing else in that formula is a 2.
  • 7B in fp16 ≈ 512 KB per token. Memorise this one number.
  • GQA divides by H/Hkv​. Decode is bandwidth-bound, so the cache is the bottleneck.

LoRA & Low-Rank Adaptation

Train a rank-8 patch, not a seven-billion-weight model.

Instead of retraining a huge grid of weights, freeze it and learn a small correction on the side. The correction is built from two thin strips: one tall and narrow, one short and wide. Multiply the strips together and you get something the same size as the original grid, but made from far fewer numbers. You only ever train the strips. When you are finished you can add the correction into the original once, and the model runs at its normal speed.

Like sewing a small patch onto a big coat. The coat is untouched and still weighs what it weighed; the patch is a few grams of thread, it is the only thing you actually made, and you can unpick it and sew a different one on tomorrow.

LoRA freezes W∈Rd×k and learns ΔW=BA with B∈Rd×r, A∈Rr×k and r≪min(d,k), typically 8 to 64. The forward pass becomes h=Wx+rα​BAx. Trainable parameters fall from dk to r(d+k): at d=k=4096 and r=8 that is 16.8M → 65.5K, a 256× cut, or 0.39% of the layer. A is initialised Gaussian and B at zero, so ΔW=0 at step 0 and training starts exactly at the base model.

This is the rank card from the Core tier being cashed in: the whole bet is that the update is intrinsically low-rank even though W is not. BA can have rank at most r, so the adapter can only move r directions. The α/r factor decouples learning rate from rank — double r and the update keeps its scale, so you do not re-tune. At inference, fold W←W+rα​BA once and the adapter costs literally nothing; keep it unmerged and you can hot-swap adapters per request. QLoRA goes further: freeze the base in 4-bit NF4, keep the LoRA path in bf16, and fine-tune a 65B model on a single 48 GB card.

You reach for it when

  • You need ten task-specific variants of one base model
  • You have one GPU and a model whose optimiser state will not fit
  • You must be able to roll a fine-tune back instantly
  • You are serving many tenants from one copy of the base weights

The trap

Two. Rank is not free quality — if the task needs genuinely new knowledge rather than new behaviour, a rank-8 update will not deliver it, and people conclude “fine-tuning does not work”. And merging: W+rα​BA is valid for one adapter at a time; merging two is not the same as running both. A quantised base must be de-quantised before a merge or you bake the rounding error in permanently.

The math dk→r(d+k) trainable · zero extra latency once merged

h=Wx+rα​BAx,B∈Rd×r,A∈Rr×kd = k = 4096, r = 8 → 16,777,216 frozen vs 65,536 trained (0.39%)

In NumPy / PyTorch

class LoRALinear(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, base, r=8, alpha=16):
        super().__init__()
        self.base = base
        self.base.weight.requires_grad_(False)   # W is frozen
        d, k = base.out_features, base.in_features
        self.A = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(r, k) * 0.01)
        self.B = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(d, r))     # B = 0 => dW = 0 at step 0
        self.s = alpha / r                          # scale, so r is not a hidden LR

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.base(x) + (x @ self.A.T @ self.B.T) * self.s

# at deploy: W += (alpha/r) * B @ A, then throw the adapter away

Where this lives in real ML code

Every “fine-tune your own model” product is this. A serving stack keeps one copy of the base in HBM and swaps rank-16 adapters of a few megabytes per customer — S-LoRA and vLLM's multi-LoRA path batch requests across different adapters on one GPU. QLoRA is why a 65B fine-tune on a single 48 GB card became a weekend job rather than a cluster booking.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

For d=k=4096 and r=16, how many trainable parameters, and what fraction of the full matrix?
131,072 — 0.78%. r(d+k)=16×8192. The full matrix is 40962=16,777,216. Handy shortcut when d=k: the fraction is just dkr(d+k)​=d2r​=409632​.
Why initialise B to zero instead of making both A and B random?
So the adapter starts as a no-op without killing its own gradient. ΔW=BA=0 at step 0, so training begins exactly at the base model. If both were zero, ∂L/∂A∝B⊤=0 and ∂L/∂B∝A⊤=0, and the pair would sit at zero forever. One zero and one random is the minimum that breaks the symmetry.
Explain out loud how LoRA connects to rank, and what α/r is actually for.
Rank caps how much a matrix can change the space. BA has rank at most r, so the update only moves r directions — the bet is that adapting behaviour needs few directions even though W is full-rank. α/r normalises the update size so that switching r=8 to r=64 does not silently multiply your effective learning rate by eight.

Say this back tomorrow

freeze W, learn BA, merge once
  • dk→r(d+k). When d=k, you train exactly 2r/d of the weights.
  • B=0 at init so the adapter starts invisible. α/r holds scale fixed as r moves.
  • Merged: zero latency. Unmerged: hot-swap per request. QLoRA = LoRA on a 4-bit frozen base.

Quantization Math

Fewer bits per number, almost the same model.

Store each weight in fewer bits. Take a group of weights, find the lowest and highest value in it, chop that span into a fixed number of evenly spaced levels, and record which level each weight landed on plus the size of one step. To use a weight you multiply its level back out. Halving the bits halves the memory. The danger is one freak value: it stretches the span, so every other weight in the group gets a much coarser step and loses detail.

Like paying every price to the nearest note in your wallet. With fives you are never more than two-fifty out; with fifties you can be out by twenty-five. The coarser the note, the worse every single purchase gets — not just the expensive one.

Affine quantisation stores q=clip(round(x/s)+z,qmin​,qmax​) and reconstructs x≈s(q−z), with s=qmax​−qmin​xmax​−xmin​​ and z chosen so real zero lands on an exact integer. Symmetric quantisation forces z=0 and is faster. Bytes per parameter: fp32 =4, fp16 and bf16 =2, int8 =1, int4 =0.5. So a 7B model is 28 GB → 14 GB → 7 GB → 3.5 GB of weights, before you add the scales back on.

Granularity is the accuracy knob. One scale per tensor is cheapest and worst; per-channel (one per output row) is standard for weights; per-group (one per 64 or 128 contiguous values) is what makes int4 usable — NF4 with group 64 plus double quantisation lands near 4.1 bits per weight, not 4.0. The blocker at scale is activation outliers: past roughly 6.7B parameters a handful of feature dimensions run 20–100× larger than the rest, so a single per-tensor int8 scale is set by them and everything else collapses into two or three levels. LLM.int8() peels those dimensions into fp16, SmoothQuant migrates the range into the weights, AWQ rescales to protect the ~1% salient channels, and GPTQ re-solves the layer output error column by column with a Hessian from calibration data.

You reach for it when

  • A model does not fit the card you actually have
  • You need headroom for the KV cache, not just the weights
  • Latency is dominated by weight loading rather than arithmetic
  • You are picking between GPTQ, AWQ and a bitsandbytes load

The trap

“Int8 is half of fp16, so it is twice as fast.” Only if you are bandwidth-bound and the kernel really computes in int8; plenty of stacks de-quantise to fp16 before the matmul, so you buy memory and no speed at all. Also, quoting “4-bit” ignores the scales: group-64 int4 with fp16 scales and zero-points is nearer 4.25–4.5 bits per weight. Always ask what the group size is.

The math bytes / param — fp32 4 · fp16 2 · int8 1 · int4 0.5

x≈s(q−z),s=qmax​−qmin​xmax​−xmin​​7B weights: fp32 28 GB · fp16 14 GB · int8 7 GB · int4 3.5 GB

In NumPy / PyTorch

# per-channel affine int8: one scale and zero-point per output row
def quantize(W, bits=8):
    qmin, qmax = 0, 2**bits - 1
    lo = W.amin(dim=1, keepdim=True)   # keepdim -- see card 33
    hi = W.amax(dim=1, keepdim=True)
    s  = (hi - lo).clamp(min=1e-8) / (qmax - qmin)
    z  = (qmin - lo / s).round()
    q  = (W / s + z).round().clamp(qmin, qmax).to(torch.uint8)
    return q, s, z

def dequantize(q, s, z):
    return (q.float() - z) * s        # x ~= s * (q - z)

Where this lives in real ML code

A 70B model is 140 GB in fp16 and will not fit an 80 GB H100; the same weights at int4 are 35 GB and do. That is the entire reason GPTQ and AWQ checkpoints dominate model hubs. bitsandbytes NF4 is the default 4-bit path in Hugging Face and the frozen base layer under QLoRA. KV-cache quantisation is the next lever — int8 KV halves the number from the previous card.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

A 13B model in fp16. How much for weights, and what does int4 buy you?
26 GB → 6.5 GB. 13×109×2 bytes =26 GB; at 0.5 bytes per parameter it is 6.5 GB, plus roughly 5–10% for group scales. That is the difference between two A100s and one consumer card — though you still have to budget the KV cache on top of it.
Why does per-tensor int8 fall apart on large language models when it was fine on ResNets?
Activation outliers. Past roughly 6.7B parameters, a handful of feature dimensions carry values twenty to a hundred times the rest. A single tensor-wide scale gets set by those outliers, so the other 99.9% of values collapse into two or three levels. Per-channel scales, LLM.int8() mixed decomposition, or SmoothQuant migrating the range into the weights all attack the same root cause.
An interviewer asks for the difference between GPTQ and AWQ in one breath.
GPTQ minimises layer output error; AWQ protects the channels that matter. GPTQ quantises weights column by column and uses a Hessian from calibration data to compensate the columns not yet done. AWQ observes that about 1% of channels are salient, judged by activation magnitude, and rescales so those survive — no backprop at all. Both are post-training, both need a small calibration set, both land around 3–4 bits.

Say this back tomorrow

x ≈ scale × (q − zero_point)
  • Bytes per parameter: 4 → 2 → 1 → 0.5. Multiply by parameter count, done.
  • Finer scales — per-tensor, per-channel, per-group — buy accuracy back for a little size.
  • Outliers set the range. Handle them or int8 collapses. GPTQ, AWQ, NF4.

38In production

RoPE: Rotations Inside Attention

Position as an angle, not as an addition.

Take the numbers in a token's vector two at a time and treat each pair as a hand on a dial. Turn every dial by an amount that depends on where the token sits in the sentence: a little for the first token, twice as much for the second, and so on. Turning never changes how long a vector is. And when two turned vectors are compared, only the difference between their turns matters, so the model feels distance rather than absolute place.

Like reading two clock hands. You do not need to know what hour either one started at — the angle between them already tells you how far apart they are. Spin both by the same amount and that angle is untouched.

RoPE splits each head vector into d/2 pairs and rotates pair i by mθi​, where m is the position and θi​=10000−2i/d. A rotation is orthogonal, so ∥Rm​x∥=∥x∥, and the load-bearing identity is (Rm​q)⊤(Rn​k)=q⊤Rn−m​k — the score depends on the relative offset n−m and on nothing else. Position enters inside the dot product instead of being added to the embedding, which is why it is applied to Q and K at every layer, and never to V.

Learned absolute embeddings are a lookup table with one row per position, so index 4097 on a model trained to 4096 simply does not exist. RoPE is a closed-form function of m, so it evaluates anywhere — but it still degrades past the trained range, because the fast pairs (large θi​) reach phase values they never met in training. Position interpolation fixes that by scaling m→m/s, squeezing 32k positions into the 4k range the model knows, at the price of resolution between nearby tokens. NTK-aware scaling and YaRN stretch the slow, long-wavelength pairs while leaving the fast ones alone, which is why a short fine-tune can push 4k to 128k.

You reach for it when

  • You are reading a modern model config and hit rope_theta
  • You need to extend a context window past the trained length
  • Long-context quality falls off a cliff and you must say why
  • Someone asks how position gets into a transformer at all

The trap

RoPE goes on Q and K only — rotating V destroys the point, because the identity that makes scores relative lives inside the dot product and V is never dotted with anything. Two more: it is applied per head, after the reshape, not on the model dimension; and “RoPE extrapolates” is overstated. It evaluates at any position but degrades fast past training length unless you interpolate or change θ.

The math O(d) per token · zero learned parameters

(Rm​q)⊤(Rn​k)=q⊤Rn−m​k,θi​=10000−2i/drotate the pairs (x₀,x₁), (x₂,x₃), … by mθᵢ — on Q and K, never on V

In NumPy / PyTorch

def rope(x, pos, base=10000.0):
    # x: (B, H, S, D) with D even.  pos: (S,)
    d   = x.shape[-1]
    inv = base ** (-torch.arange(0, d, 2).float() / d)   # theta_i
    ang = pos[:, None] * inv[None, :]              # (S, D/2) -- broadcasting again
    cos, sin = ang.cos(), ang.sin()
    x1, x2 = x[..., 0::2], x[..., 1::2]
    return torch.stack([x1*cos - x2*sin,
                        x1*sin + x2*cos], dim=-1).flatten(-2)

q, k = rope(q, pos), rope(k, pos)     # V is never rotated

Where this lives in real ML code

Llama, Mistral, Qwen and Gemma all use RoPE, and most context-length announcements are a rope_theta change plus a short fine-tune: Llama-2 shipped θbase​=104 at 4k, Llama-3.1 uses 5×105 at 128k. Load a checkpoint with a mismatched rope_scaling config and the model is coherent for a few hundred tokens and then turns to noise — a bug that looks like a ruined fine-tune and is really a wrong angle.

Interview drill 3 questions · click to reveal

Why is ∥Rm​x∥=∥x∥ the load-bearing property?
Because it keeps the score scale independent of position. Rm​ is orthogonal, so rotating never inflates or shrinks a vector. Position therefore cannot change how loud a token is, only how it aligns — unlike additive position embeddings, which perturb magnitude and bleed into the content signal.
A model trained at 4k is asked for 32k. What happens with learned absolute embeddings, and what happens with RoPE?
Absolute: it crashes or reads a garbage row. RoPE: it runs, then degrades. A learned table has no row 4097. RoPE is a formula, so it evaluates — but the high-frequency pairs wrap into phases never seen in training and attention flattens out. Position interpolation (m→m/8), or NTK-aware / YaRN scaling plus a short fine-tune, is the standard repair.
Explain out loud, in one sentence each, why RoPE is relative and why it is free.
Relative: rotating q by m and k by n leaves q⊤Rn−m​k, so the score sees only n−m. Free: there are no learned parameters and it is an O(d) elementwise pass over Q and K — cheaper than the projections it follows, and it composes with the KV cache because a cached key was already rotated at its own position and never needs touching again.

Say this back tomorrow

rotate by position; the dot product keeps only the difference
  • Pairs of dimensions, rotated by mθi​ with θi​=10000−2i/d.
  • Rotations preserve length, so (Rm​q)⊤(Rn​k)=q⊤Rn−m​k.
  • Q and K only, never V. Extend context with position interpolation, NTK-aware or YaRN scaling.
